app.tagline: Buy and sell crypto, your way.

settings.title: Settings
settings.subtitle: Your identity, your rules. Stored on your device, never on our servers.

display_name.heading: Display name
display_name.explain: A friendly label that shows up next to your avatar. It does NOT replace your public key — that's always shown in parentheses, and that's the part people should trust. You can change this at any time.
display_name.reminder_body: Anyone can use any name. The short key in parentheses — for example (BLT7gHu8mn…A9bb) — is what really identifies you, and it cannot be copied by anyone else. Always check the key when you're trading.

broadcast_err.no_account: Saved locally. Publishing will be available once your account is registered.
broadcast_err.locked: Session is locked. Sign in again to broadcast.

display_name.clear_confirm_prompt: Remove your display name from this device? You can set it again anytime.
display_name.broadcast_ok_detail: Your display name is now published for everyone to see.

endpoints.heading: RPC endpoints
endpoints.explain: The network nodes Morphit talks to for reading and writing data. The app tries them in order of fastest response. Add your own or a community-run node.
endpoints.duplicate: That endpoint is already in the list.
endpoints.at_least_one: Please keep at least one endpoint.
endpoints.reset_confirm_prompt: Reset all custom RPC endpoints to defaults?

session.heading: Session
session.explain: Sign out when you're done. Your posting + memo keys will be wiped from memory; the encrypted keystore on your device is untouched.
session.confirm_prompt: Sign out of this device? Your posting + memo keys will be wiped from memory. You'll need to unlock again to trade.
session.autolock_help: Automatically lock your session after this long with no activity. Locking clears your keys from memory; your encrypted keystore stays on this device so you can unlock with your password when you return.

change_password.heading: Change password
change_password.help: Replace your keystore password without signing out. Your keys stay the same; only the password that decrypts them changes.
change_password.strength_common: This password is too common. Pick something less guessable.
change_password.strength_trivial: This password is too simple. Try a longer mix of words.
change_password.strength_short: Consider a longer password — 12+ characters is much harder to guess.

err.new_password_too_short: New password must be at least 8 characters.
err.same_password: New password must be different from your current password.
err.locked: Your session is locked. Unlock first, then try again.
err.bad_old_password: That doesn't match your current password. Try again.
err.mismatch: The two new passwords don't match.
err.internal: Something went wrong. Your old password still works; please try again.

nostr_url.heading: Nostr link
nostr_url.explain: Optional. Add your Nostr profile URL and a small Nostr icon appears next to your username everywhere on Morphit. Helps people reach you outside this marketplace.
nostr_url.label: Your Nostr URL
nostr_url.hint_empty: Leave blank if you do not want a Nostr link shown.

error.too_long: Too long. Keep it under 512 characters.
error.invalid_scheme: Only nostr:, https://, and http:// URLs are allowed.
error.malformed: That does not look like a valid URL.

nostr_url.need_display_name: Set a display name first. Your profile broadcast includes both.
nostr_url.reminder_body: Once published, the Nostr icon appears next to your username on every order, every feedback entry, every chat message — on every Morphit instance, not just this one. Other users tap it to open your Nostr profile in their preferred client.

blurt_media_url.heading: Blurt.media profile URL
blurt_media_url.explain: A link to your profile on blurt.media, the popular Blurt frontend. Displayed alongside your username everywhere on Morphit. Optional.
blurt_media_url.label: Blurt.media URL
blurt_media_url.hint_empty: Paste your blurt.media profile URL here, or leave blank.

error.wrong_host: Only blurt.media URLs are accepted here.

blurt_media_url.broadcast_ok: Broadcast — visible across Morphit after next block.
blurt_media_url.need_display_name: Set a display name first — your profile op carries both fields together.
blurt_media_url.reminder_body: Your Morphit identity works fine without this URL. It's a courtesy link for people who want to see your Blurt.media presence from your Morphit profile.

notifications.heading: Notifications
notifications.explain: Morphit pings you when something happens — an order fills, a chat message arrives, feedback lands. All of these are off-by-default where annoying-by-default, and opt-in where high-signal. Never when you're already looking at the page.
notifications.category_heading: What do you want to be told about?
notifications.category_order_help: Your order filled, expired, or was replaced by a counter-offer. Recommended on — highest signal-to-noise.
notifications.category_chat_help: New message in an active trade chat. Coalesced: 3 messages in 30 seconds is one notification.
notifications.category_feedback_help: Someone left you feedback, or responded to feedback you left them.
notifications.channel_ambient_help: Always on. Zero permissions, never audible. Works on the tab you're looking at.
notifications.channel_native_help: OS-native notification when a new event arrives and this tab isn't focused. Asks permission the first time we need it.
notifications.channel_push_help: Also notify when Morphit is not open at all. Requires a push service — you can choose self-hosted, standard browser, or off.
notifications.channel_audio_help: Short sound when a notification fires. Only plays when this tab isn't focused.
notifications.channel_vibrate_help: Short vibration pattern when a notification fires. Ignored on devices that don't support it.
notifications.quiet_explain: Silence audio and push during these hours. Visual channels (title bar, favicon, badge) still update — they're ambient, not alerts.
notifications.mute_until_unmute: Mute until I turn it back on
notifications.permission_banner_body: You just got a new {category} event. Want to know about future ones even when you're not looking at Morphit?
notifications.permission_denied_explain: You previously declined notifications. If you'd like to enable them, you'll need to change your browser's site permission for this page, then toggle the setting above.
notifications.hint_badging_unsupported: Your browser doesn't support OS-level app badges. Install Morphit as an app to enable this.
notifications.hint_notifications_unsupported: Your browser doesn't support desktop notifications.
notifications.push_error_push_disabled: This instance's operator has not enabled push delivery yet. Falling back to in-tab notifications.
notifications.push_error_permission_denied: You declined the browser's notification permission. To enable push later, allow notifications for this site in your browser settings.
notifications.push_error_not_supported: Your browser does not support Web Push. Try a recent Firefox, Chrome, or Edge.
notifications.push_error_unreachable: Could not reach the operator's relay. Check your connection and try again.
notifications.push_error_no_vapid_key: The operator's relay did not return a push key. Push may be temporarily disabled.
notifications.push_error_subscribe_failed: Subscription failed. Try again, or check your browser's site permissions.
notifications.push_error_internal: Something went wrong on the operator's relay. Try again in a moment.
notifications.push_error_signature_required: This instance requires a signed subscribe request. Make sure your account is unlocked and try again.
notifications.push_error_signature_invalid: Your signature was rejected by the relay. Try unlocking your account again, then retry.
notifications.push_error_locked_session: Your session is locked. Unlock your account first to enable push notifications.

hidden_accounts.heading: Hidden accounts
hidden_accounts.explain: Orders from these accounts don't appear on your orderbook view. You can unhide anyone at any time.
hidden_accounts.scope_note: Hiding is local to this browser. It doesn't ban anyone from the protocol, doesn't notify them, and doesn't affect what other Morphit instances see.
hidden_accounts.unhide_all_confirm: Unhide all {count} accounts? This will make their orders visible again on your orderbook view.

avatar.heading: Avatar
avatar.explain: Replace your default heart identicon with your own image. Stored on-chain inside your profile op, just like your display name and social links.
avatar.guidance_filetypes: Accepts SVG, WebP, JPEG, PNG, or GIF.
avatar.guidance_dimensions: Ideal source: a square image at least 96×96 pixels. Anything larger will be resized down to 96×96 for you; anything smaller will look grainy.
avatar.guidance_filesize: Source file size: up to 5 MB. Larger images will be downsampled to 96×96 automatically, so even a phone photo straight from your camera works fine.
avatar.guidance_size: Raster images are automatically re-encoded to WebP at high quality. SVGs are minified losslessly. The final payload must fit under 3 KB.
avatar.guidance_svg_tips: SVG tip: a square viewBox (e.g. 0 0 100 100) renders best. Scripts, external references, and HTML-in-SVG are stripped automatically for security.
avatar.permanence_body: Once broadcast, your avatar is public on the Blurt blockchain forever. It cannot be deleted, only replaced. Never upload an image you wouldn't want publicly associated with your account for the rest of time — photos of faces, in particular, are a privacy consideration given modern face-recognition tools.
avatar.preview_getting_large: Getting close to the size limit — consider a simpler image or smaller source.
avatar.need_display_name: Set and broadcast your display name first before changing your avatar.

blocked_accounts.heading: Blocked accounts
blocked_accounts.explain: Accounts you have blocked cannot send you chat messages on Morphit. Blocking is on-chain and visible to anyone scraping Blurt, but Morphit does not tell the blocked person.
blocked_accounts.scope_note: This list is derived from on-chain blocks. Refresh to pull the latest from the indexer.
blocked_accounts.refresh_aria: Refresh the blocked accounts list from the indexer
blocked_accounts.unblock_failed: Could not unblock. Please check your connection and try again.
blocked_accounts.locked_hint: Unlock your session to unblock accounts.

syndication.heading: Syndication
syndication.explain: Morphit can publish announcement posts to your Blurt blog when you take certain actions. These are signed by your posting key — Morphit holds nothing on your behalf.
syndication.first_trade_label: Auto-announce my first trade to the @morphit community
syndication.first_trade_help: When you leave feedback for your first-ever Morphit trade, also publish a short "I joined Morphit" post to the @morphit community on Blurt. Posts only once per account, ever. Per-order syndication is a separate per-submission checkbox on the order form.
syndication.pitch_body: Syndication of your trades is everything. More eyes on your offers means more trading partners, plus upvote rewards going directly into your Blurt Wallet. Off = nothing public.

privacy.heading: Privacy
privacy.cross_page_trade_events_help: When on, Morphit watches your recent chats for trade events (address shared, funds sent) so badges update on /my/orders without you opening the chat. This briefly decrypts incoming messages in the background. Turn off if you prefer the chat page itself to be the only place trade events are processed.

hardware_key.heading: Hardware key
hardware_key.explain: Bind a YubiKey to your keystore as a second unlock method, or as your only unlock method. Adds a strong second factor that a stolen password alone can't bypass.
hardware_key.unsupported_title: Your browser doesn't support hardware keys
hardware_key.unsupported_body: YubiKey unlock requires WebHID, which is currently only available in Chrome, Edge, Brave, and other Chromium-based browsers. Firefox and Safari don't expose this API. You can keep using your password as before.
hardware_key.seed_only_note: Hardware keys are only available when you have a persisted keystore. You're using seed-only mode — no envelope is stored on this device, so there's nothing to bind a key to.
hardware_key.soften_explain: After this, you'll be able to unlock with EITHER your YubiKey OR a password. Set a new password below; you'll need your YubiKey one more time to apply the change.
hardware_key.backup_warning_title: Have you backed up your seed phrase and your keys?
hardware_key.backup_warning_body: Adding a YubiKey re-encrypts your keystore. If you lose access to your YubiKey AND forget your password, only your 12-word seed phrase can recover this account. Please make sure it's written down somewhere safe before continuing.
hardware_key.backup_confirm_label: Yes, my seed phrase is backed up safely.
hardware_key.slot_hint: Most users program HMAC-SHA1 challenge-response into slot 2 — slot 1 usually holds Yubico OTP. Use Yubico Authenticator to configure your key first if you haven't already.
hardware_key.harden_warning_title: This is a one-way switch — proceed with care.
hardware_key.harden_warning_body: After hardening, your password will no longer unlock this keystore. Only your YubiKey will. If you lose your YubiKey, only your 12-word seed phrase can recover this account. You can always soften back later, but it requires a YubiKey tap.
hardware_key.harden_confirm_label: I understand. Without my YubiKey or seed phrase, this account is permanently inaccessible.

install.heading: Install Morphit as an app
install.explain: Add Morphit to your home screen for one-tap access. The app launches in fullscreen, works offline, and gets the same updates as the website. No data leaves your device that wouldn't already.
install.manual_intro: Your browser doesn't expose a one-click install. Use the manual path:
install.manual_chrome: Chrome / Edge: tap the address bar's install icon, or use the browser menu → Install Morphit.
install.manual_safari: Safari (macOS / iOS): tap the Share button, then "Add to Home Screen".
install.manual_firefox: Firefox Android: tap the menu (︙), then "Install". Firefox desktop doesn't support PWA install — use Chromium-based browsers.

account_name.heading: Blurt account name
account_name.explain: Morphit needs to know your Blurt account name so it can recognize your trades, messages, and on-chain activity. If you imported a posting key with the account name, this is already set. If you imported a seed phrase or keyfile, set it here.
account_name.locked_explain: To change this, sign out, then re-import with a different account.
account_name.input_hint: Without the @. We'll verify your posting key matches this account on the Blurt chain before saving.
account_name.error_locked: Unlock your keystore first to set your account name.
account_name.error_bad_format: Account names use lowercase letters, digits, dashes, and dots — 3 to 16 characters, starting with a letter.
account_name.error_not_found: We couldn't find @{account} on the Blurt chain. Check the spelling.
account_name.error_key_mismatch: Your posting key doesn't match @{account}'s posting authority. Check that you imported the right keys.
account_name.error_chain_unreachable: We couldn't reach the Blurt chain. Check your connection and try again.

import_landing_banner.title: Almost done — pick your @account so the orderbook recognizes you
import_landing_banner.body: We brought you here because seed/keyfile imports don't carry your Blurt account name. Set it once below and we'll verify it on-chain.

preferences.heading: Preferences
preferences.explain: Morphit remembers a few of your form values so you don't have to refill them every time you post. Stored only on this device — never sent to any server, never put on chain.
preferences.empty: No preferences saved yet. Post an order and your fiat currency and region will be remembered for next time.
preferences.clear_confirm_body: Clear your saved fiat currency and region? You'll just need to pick them again next time you post.

errors.too_long: Too long — please keep it to 40 characters or fewer.
errors.control_char: That name contains a control character that isn't allowed.
errors.invisible_char: That name contains an invisible or direction-override character that isn't allowed.
errors.leading_at: Can't start a display name with "@" — it looks too much like an account handle. Try a different first character.
errors.impersonation: That name could be confused with a reserved project account. Try a different name.

profile.given_error: Couldn't load the reviews this user has left.
profile.no_given_yet: Nothing yet. This user has not left feedback on any counterparties.
profile.rss_subscribe_title: Get notified via RSS when this trader posts a new buy or sell order. Note: polling a per-trader feed is slightly more revealing than the global feed.
profile.feedback_suppressed_chip: Not counted toward rating — reviewers flagged as related

my_balance.low_blurt_hint: Your liquid BLURT is running low. Top up to keep posting orders.
my_balance.low_mana_hint: Your MANA is low. Each chain action consumes a small amount; it regenerates over about 5 days. If you're posting often, top up some BLURT and power it up.

pnl.export_hint: Downloads a CSV of your BLURT transfers, fees, and Featured-bid activity.

home.hero_title: Privately trade Monero, Bitcoin and more with Fiat currencies+
home.hero_body: Morphit connects buyers and sellers directly. No KYC, non-custodial, no cookies, E2EE, no logging, no escrow, private by default, open source, fully-distributed+

non_custodial.title: Non-custodial
non_custodial.body: Your coins move directly between you and your trading partner. Morphit never touches them.

no_kyc.title: No ID, no email
no_kyc.body: A keypair generated on your device is your whole account. Nothing else needed.

uncensorable.title: Unstoppable
uncensorable.body: Reachable on the clearnet, Tor, Lokinet, and I2P. No central server can take it offline.

grandma.title: Built for humans
grandma.body: If it isn't clear in five seconds, we didn't do our job. If you get stuck, we explain.

home.returning_user_prompt: Already have a Blurt account or set up Morphit on another device?
home.networks_body: Same site, same code, four ways to reach it. If one path is blocked, another works.

onboarding.title: Let's set up your keys
onboarding.intro: Your Morphit account is a pair of cryptographic keys. They are made right here on your device and never leave it. If you lose them, no one can recover them — not even us. That's the price of true privacy.

path_reputation.title: Build Reputation
path_reputation.body: One identity over time. Your successful trades earn a public track record that makes people trust you. Recommended for most users.

path_anonymous.title: Maximum Anonymity
path_anonymous.body: A fresh identity every trade. Nothing links your trades together. Best for Monero users who prioritize unlinkability — but you start from zero reputation every time.

onboarding.generating: Generating your keys securely on your device…
onboarding.generated_body: Before you do anything else, back them up. If you lose them, your account is gone forever. We warned you — this is the tradeoff for keys only you control.
onboarding.this_is_you: This is how you appear to others

backup.title: Back up your keys
backup.seed_hint: 12 words. In order. On paper. In KeePass(.info). Make a backup copy too. Store the 12 words somewhere SAFE. Do not photograph them. Do not email them to yourself.
backup.confirm_wrote_down: I wrote the seed down on paper
backup.confirm_understand: I'll keep these 12 words safe — I know they're the only way back into my account.
backup.password_hint: Choose a strong passphrase. This encrypts the backup file — not the keys on Morphit.
backup.continue: I've backed up my keys — continue
backup.blocked: Please confirm both boxes before continuing.
backup.password_too_short: Password must be at least 10 characters.
backup.keyfile_explain: Optionally download an encrypted backup of your keys. Same password as above. Store the file somewhere safe (USB drive, cloud you trust, another device) as an alternate path back into your account if the browser storage is wiped.
backup.password_strength_common: This password is among the most common — pick something unique to you.
backup.password_strength_trivial: Sequential or repeated patterns are easy to guess. Mix it up.
backup.password_strength_short: Consider a longer password (12+ characters recommended).
backup.persist_failed: Couldn't save your encrypted keystore to this device. Storage may be unavailable. Choose 'Seed every time' instead, or try again.
backup.password_strength_too_simple: Mix in numbers, symbols, or uppercase — or make it 12+ characters.

print_card.aria: Print a paper backup card with your 12 words
print_card.helper_hint: Opens your browser's print dialog. You can print to paper or save as PDF.
print_card.title: My Morphit backup card
print_card.subtitle: Keep this paper safe — it is the only way back into your account.
print_card.warning_body: Anyone who finds these 12 words can take everything in your Morphit account. Store this paper somewhere only you can reach — a safe, a locked drawer, or a secure deposit box. Don't photograph it. Don't email it. Don't store it in cloud notes.
print_card.instructions: If you ever lose access to your device, type these 12 words into Morphit's import flow on a new device to recover your account.

import.title: Import existing keys
import.body: Already have a Blurt account? Pick how you have your key stored. If you've never used Blurt before, go back and create a new account instead.
import.seed_hint: For users who set up Morphit (or another wallet that ships our seed format) before. If you don't have a 12-word seed, use one of the other tabs.
import.keyfile_hint: An encrypted .json file you exported from Morphit on another device, or a backup you saved.

posting_only.warning_body: If you only have a posting WIF (no master password or seed), you can paste it here. We'll encrypt it on this device with a password you choose. You'll be able to read, post, and trade — but not change account keys (that needs the active or owner key).
posting_only.account_hint: Without the @. We'll check that this account exists on Blurt and that the posting key matches.
posting_only.wif_hint: Starts with 5 (legacy) or P5 (newer). Never shared with the operator — encrypted on this device only.
posting_only.new_password_hint: At least 8 characters. Used to unlock Morphit on this device. Not your Blurt password.

confirm.title: Let's confirm you wrote it down
confirm.body: Type a few specific words from the seed you just saved. This makes sure you really have the phrase written down, not just that you clicked a box.
confirm.wrong: That's not quite right. Double-check your written copy of the seed.

register_name.title: Choose your account name
register_name.subtitle: This is the name people see when they trade with you. It's permanent — choose something you're happy to use for a long time.
register_name.field_hint: 3–16 lowercase letters, digits, or dashes. Must start with a letter. No spaces, no dots, no capitals.

availability.taken: That name is already taken. Pick another.
availability.rejected_generic: That name isn't allowed. Try a different one.
availability.unreachable: Can't reach the registration service right now. Check your connection or try again in a moment.

reasons.bad_chars: Only lowercase letters, digits, and dashes are allowed.
reasons.consecutive_dashes: Two dashes in a row are not allowed.
reasons.leading_trailing_dash: The name can't start or end with a dash.
reasons.reserved: That name is reserved. Pick another.
reasons.rate_limited: Too many checks in a short time. Wait a minute and try again.

fee.title: Registration is free for you
fee.hint: Account creation is free — Morphit covers the network cost.
fee.body: We pay the on-chain creation fee — you don't need any BLURT to sign up.

what_is_morphit.a: Morphit is a peer-to-peer marketplace where people trade cash for Bitcoin, Monero, and BLURT directly with each other. Morphit never holds your money and never asks who you are. It is a bulletin board, not a bank.

is_it_safe.a: Safer than platforms that hold your funds — because Morphit can't lose or freeze what it never had. The real risk is your trading partner, so always check their reputation before agreeing to trade. Morphit shows you their completed trades, feedback, and how long they've been around.

vs_others.q: How is Morphit different from LocalMonero, LocalBitcoins, or Haveno/Retoswap?
vs_others.a:
Short version: Morphit goes further on decentralization, privacy, and non-custody than any of them — and deliberately does less in exchange.

LocalBitcoins (RIP, 2023) and LocalMonero (closed 2024) were centralized companies with custodial escrow. When a trade went wrong, their human arbitrators held the coins and decided who got them. When the companies shut down — by regulator pressure or business decision — their entire user base, reputations, dispute history, and ongoing trades vanished overnight. Morphit cannot be shut down in the same way: there are no central arbitrators, no custodial wallets, no company bank account to freeze. Every order lives on Blurt, every trade is peer-to-peer, and anyone can run an indexer or frontend. Multiple instances on four networks (clearnet, Tor, Lokinet, I2P) mean blocking one node does nothing.

Haveno (and its fork Retoswap) is much closer in spirit — non-custodial, P2P, no KYC. The big differences: Haveno is a desktop-only Java/JavaFX application tied to the Monero blockchain for its 2-of-3 multisig escrow, and needs you to run (or connect to) a seednode. Morphit runs in any browser, on any phone, with no install; uses Blurt (not Monero) for its on-chain coordination layer, which is faster and far cheaper per action (~free vs. Monero's per-op fees); and ships with built-in Tor, Lokinet, and I2P reachability rather than relying on you to configure it. Haveno trades involve arbitrated escrow, which is strong but requires trusted arbitrators per market. Morphit v1 is pure reputation-based bulletin board — no escrow, no arbitrator, full responsibility on the traders to pick partners with real track records. That's a more conservative safety model, but also fewer centralized choke points and no arbitrator role that a government could pressure.

On privacy: Morphit pushes harder than any of the above on transport, storage, and chat.
• Transport: four parallel networks, all first-class (not just an 'onion mode').
• Storage: nothing about you lives on Morphit's servers — keys are in your browser, orders are on Blurt, chats are on Blurt as ciphertext only. Haveno stores trade history on your desktop; Morphit matches that while also letting you move to any device with just your 12-word seed.
• Chat: end-to-end encrypted using X25519 key agreement plus ChaCha20-Poly1305 (from libsodium), with a per-message ephemeral key. LocalBitcoins/LocalMonero chats were visible to staff. Haveno chats are end-to-end encrypted. Morphit chat is encrypted on your device, stored as ciphertext on the Blurt blockchain, and decryptable only by the two participants — operators and chain observers see nothing. We deliberately chose a simple, fast, low-bundle-weight ECIES design.

On non-custody: LocalBitcoins/LocalMonero held your coins during a trade. Haveno/Retoswap lock your coins in multisig during a trade. Morphit never touches them at any point, period — the seller sends directly to the buyer when payment is confirmed. That is more trust placed on reputation, less on cryptography; honest about the tradeoff.

On arbitration: LocalBitcoins/LocalMonero arbitrators could overrule feedback. Haveno arbitrators could redirect multisig payouts. Morphit has no arbitrator role at all; feedback is permanent and signed on chain. If you scam someone, your public key carries that feedback forever; you cannot appeal to a human. That's a strong disincentive for repeat scammers and zero protection for first-time ones — hence the emphasis on checking account age and reputation.

What Morphit doesn't have that they do: escrow, human arbitration, per-market moderation. **Morphit will never offer any of these.** Reintroducing escrow, multisig, or arbitration would reintroduce the middleman this project exists to remove. Morphit's advantage is that it's lean, portable, browser-native, fully decentralized at every layer, and impossible to shut down — and its tradeoff is that you trade on immutable, provable reputation.

vs_atomic_swap_dexes.q: How is Morphit different from Bisq or BasicSwap?
vs_atomic_swap_dexes.a:
Bisq and BasicSwap are kindred projects in the no-middleman peer-to-peer space, but make different architectural choices than Morphit.

**Bisq** is a long-running peer-to-peer marketplace with the same architectural pattern as Haveno: desktop Java application, 2-of-3 multisig escrow during trades, Tor for transport, arbitrated disputes when something goes wrong. Bisq has been compromised twice with user funds stolen — the kind of risk Morphit avoids by never touching user funds in the first place. Bisq also requires you to lock up BSQ collateral before you can list orders. Morphit locks up nothing from anyone.

**BasicSwap** takes a structurally different approach: cross-chain atomic swaps directly between two wallets, no escrow, no arbitrator, no central server. Aligned with Morphit on the "no middleman" principle. The tradeoffs differ from Morphit's tradeoffs:

• Installation gate. BasicSwap is a desktop app (or Docker setup); users have to install and run it before they can even browse the orderbook or see live offers. Morphit's orderbook is a public web page at /orderbook on any instance, browsable from any phone or computer without installing anything.

• Heavy local infrastructure. BasicSwap typically runs full nodes for every chain it trades — Bitcoin, Monero, Litecoin, and so on. First-time sync can take hours to days; ongoing storage, CPU, RAM, and bandwidth costs are substantial. Morphit is a browser tab.

• Slow swap completion. Cross-chain atomic swaps need multiple block confirmations on both chains to be safe; a single BTC ↔ XMR atomic swap typically takes 30 minutes to several hours of locked coins waiting for time-locks to clear. Morphit's coordination layer finalizes each step on the next Blurt block — about 3 seconds — so the workflow itself never stalls. (The actual asset transfer still depends on whatever chain or payment method the two parties chose; Morphit doesn't claim faster settlement of the underlying coins — just faster coordination on top of whatever the parties chose.)

• No in-app reputation. BasicSwap has no built-in, network-wide feedback or rating system. Morphit feedback is signed on-chain and follows your public key forever — you carry your reputation with you across every instance.

• No E2EE chat. BasicSwap doesn't ship a messaging layer for negotiating, asking questions, or sending payment details — those conversations happen outside the protocol. Morphit chat is end-to-end encrypted on the device and stored as ciphertext on the chain.

• Both parties online during the swap. The atomic-swap protocol requires both wallets to be live for the full multi-step exchange; if your counterparty stalls or disappears mid-swap, you wait out the refund timelock (often hours) to recover your coins. Morphit trades don't require simultaneous presence — you post an order, the counterparty acts when they're ready, and either party can return to the trade on their own schedule.

• Crypto-only, no fiat. BasicSwap trades crypto-to-crypto only. Morphit supports fiat ↔ crypto in whatever payment method two parties agree on (bank transfer, cash, gift card, in-game currency, whatever they prefer).

• Mandatory client updates. BasicSwap users must keep their client current to stay compatible with peers, and updates can involve resync work. Morphit auto-updates in the browser like any web page; operators upgrade their server-side instance independently.

BasicSwap's strength — true cross-chain atomic swaps with no middleman — is real and a beautiful piece of cryptographic engineering. Morphit makes a different choice: a coordination + reputation layer that works for fiat and crypto, accessible from any browser on any device, where the privacy work happens in transport (Tor/Lokinet/I2P) and chat (E2EE) rather than in the swap protocol itself. Both designs are valid; they serve different users.

video_tutorial.a: Yes — we host short video tutorials on blurt.media, the decentralized PeerTube instance for the Blurt community. Watch at https://blurt.media (search for "Morphit"). We link out rather than embed because video embeds come with trade-offs for privacy: a PeerTube iframe would expose your IP to other viewers in the P2P swarm. Opening blurt.media in a new tab keeps you in control. If you use a VPN or Tor Browser (recommended), your IP is already protected and the embed trade-off disappears.

signup_requirements.q: What do I need to sign up?
signup_requirements.a: Nothing. No email, no phone number, no name. Your browser generates a cryptographic keypair on your device — that is your entire account. Write down the 12-word recovery seed and you're done.

how_to_buy.a: Open the orderbook, filter by the coin you want and your country. Pick a seller with good reputation, open a chat, agree on the details. You pay the seller in your chosen fiat method (cash, bank transfer, etc.), and they send you the crypto. The trade timer gives you several days to complete payment.

how_to_sell.a: Post an order listing what you're selling, where you are, and which payment methods you accept. A buyer will open a chat with you to agree on details. When you confirm you received their payment, you send them the crypto. Leave honest feedback when done — it helps everyone.

fees.a:
Three things to know:

1. Morphit never takes a cut of your trade itself. The price you and your counterparty agree on is the price you receive — nothing is skimmed. Morphit isn't an escrow and doesn't touch your funds.

2. Posting an order costs a small network fee:
   • **$0.25 USD-equivalent** if you pay in BTC or XMR (full price)
   • **$0.125 USD-equivalent** if you pay in BLURT (a deliberate 50% discount)
   The discount exists because Morphit's coordination layer runs on Blurt, and we want the BLURT economy to thrive. Paying in BLURT is the default option, costs half as much, and counts toward loyalty-milestone Blurt Power rewards (see "How loyalty rewards work"). The compose screen shows the exact amount in your chosen currency before you sign — no surprises.

3. Your very first buy order is free. We waive the network fee on your first-ever buy — a small welcome gift so new traders can try Morphit risk-free. See "Is my first order really free?" for the details.

There's also an optional "featured" slot you can bid on if you want your order to stand out — a per-hour cost that you only pay if you actively want the visibility.

A note on the spam-deterrent escalation: post a lot of orders quickly (4+ in a 24-hour window) and the per-order fee starts climbing. This is the anti-Sybil tier — it bites spammers far more than real users, who rarely post more than 2-3 listings in a day. The compose screen shows you the current tier multiplier before you sign so there's no surprise. The Sybil escalation only applies to BLURT-paid orders; BTC and XMR fees are flat at the base rate.

trade_goods_services.q: Can I trade goods or services on Morphit, like fruit trees or vintage records?
trade_goods_services.a:
Yes — but with a specific shape that takes a moment to grasp. Morphit's order model is always **a tradable asset (BTC, XMR, BLURT, USDT, BCH, or LTC) on one side, and something else on the other side**. The "something else" can be:

• A **fiat currency** (USD, EUR, MXN, COP, NGN — any country's money)
• A **different cryptocurrency** (e.g. paying with BTC for an order whose asset is XMR)
• **Goods or services**, via the `Barter (goods)` payment method

**To trade orange trees for XMR**, you would post: side=`buy`, asset=`XMR`, payment_methods=`[Barter (goods)]`, fiat_currency=`USD` (or whatever pricing reference you and the counterparty agree to), and put the specifics in the `terms` field — for example: `"50 healthy orange tree saplings, 30cm+ tall, picked up at my farm in Querétaro, MX. Will release XMR after delivery."` Buyers of orange trees who happen to have XMR will respond.

**To trade BTC for a cherry tree**, post: side=`sell`, asset=`BTC`, payment_methods=`[Barter (goods)]`, fiat_currency=`USD` (reference price), terms=`"Will accept one mature cherry tree (3+ years, healthy) as payment for 0.001 BTC. Delivery to Mexico City."`

**What you cannot model directly**: goods-for-goods trades (orange trees for moringa trees, with no crypto involved). One side of every Morphit order has to be BTC, XMR, BLURT, or USDT — that's how the chain anchors the trade and how feedback gets attached to a real on-chain action. For pure barter without crypto, use a different platform.

**Why this constraint?** Three reasons:

1. **Reputation needs anchoring.** Feedback is signed against an order op on Blurt. The order op references a specific divisible asset (with a quantity, a price, a fee). Pure goods don't fit this shape — there's no "how much of an orange tree" question.

2. **The marketplace works because most orders price in a common unit.** A buyer scanning the orderbook for `XMR/USD < $300` gets a clean list. If half the orders priced in fruit trees and the other half in haircuts, search and matching break down.

3. **Disputes are easier when one side is provable on-chain.** If you sent BTC and didn't get the cherry tree, the BTC transfer is on-chain forever. The seller can't deny receiving payment. With crypto on at least one side, every Morphit trade has a hard receipt for one half.

**About payment methods like Bitso, Zelle, PayPal**: these are **fiat-side rails** — they describe HOW the fiat (or a fiat-denominated reference price) gets transferred. "Bitso transfer for moringa trees" doesn't fit the model: Bitso transfers MXN, not moringa trees. Closest model: post a buy XMR order paid via Bitso, then separately use that XMR to buy moringa trees off-platform. Two trades, not one.

**Vice-versa combinations**: every combination of `(side, asset, payment_methods, fiat_currency)` works as long as the asset is one of BTC/XMR/BLURT/USDT. The free-form `terms` field describes what the trade actually involves on the human-readable side. Common combinations:

• Buy/sell BTC for USD via PayPal
• Buy/sell XMR for cash in person
• Buy/sell BLURT for BTC (crypto-for-crypto)
• Buy/sell USDT (on Tron, Ethereum, Solana, or BSC) for fiat via Wise or in-person cash
• Buy XMR for orange trees (barter, with USD reference price)
• Sell BTC for a cherry tree (barter, with USD reference price)
• Sell USDT for raw garlic (barter, with USD reference price)
• Sell XMR for an in-person cash exchange (`payment_methods=[cash]`)

order_timeouts.q: How long do orders stay open?
order_timeouts.a: Orders stay visible for up to 90 days by default (you can change this 1–90 days). You have 15 minutes after posting to replace an order for typos; after that it's locked. Trades themselves happen off-platform — Morphit coordinates the order match, but you and your counterparty agree on the payment timeline directly via the encrypted chat. Most pairs settle within hours; long-running disputes are rare because feedback discipline incentivizes both sides to close out quickly. If your order expires without a match, you can re-list it from /my/orders with one click.

order_editing.q: Can I fix or cancel an order after posting?
order_editing.a: You have 15 minutes after posting to replace an order (for typos or wrong numbers). After 15 minutes, or as soon as someone expresses interest in trading, the order is locked. You can still cancel it — cancellation is its own on-chain action, always allowed before a trade begins. Technically: Blurt's `custom_json` ops are permanent and not editable at the protocol level, so Morphit handles 'edits' by posting a tiny replacement op that references the original. Both versions live on chain forever — anyone can audit the full history — but indexers only accept replacements posted within the 15-minute window. Why 15 minutes? A longer window is an attack: a seller could post favorable terms, wait for a buyer to start negotiating, then silently worsen them. Fifteen minutes is enough to catch a typo during proofreading, short enough that no real conversation has started.

chat_privacy.a:
Your chat content is fully private — encrypted end-to-end between you and your counterparty. Only your two devices hold the keys to decrypt.

What's private:
• Message text
• Any payment details, addresses, or negotiation you exchange

What's not private (metadata, visible on chain):
• Your counterparty's account handle
• Timestamps of when each message was sent
• Approximate message size

Cryptography used:
• X25519 key agreement (elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman)
• ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption
• Fresh ephemeral key per message

These are standard, well-audited primitives (from libsodium). The protocol is a simple ECIES design documented in ADR-0015. If your threat model requires stronger properties like per-message forward secrecy, use a dedicated secure messenger — good options include **Matrix/Element**, **Session**, **Keybase**, and **Signal**. (Morphit complements but doesn't replace a dedicated secure messenger.)

monero_amount_jitter.q: Why does Morphit randomize my transfer amount?
monero_amount_jitter.a: Identical amounts on a public chain create a fingerprint linking your orderbook post to the on-chain transfer. Morphit adds a tiny random tail (well under a cent at typical prices) to every transfer to defeat this. Shipped for XMR originally; cp26 generalizes to every transparent asset — BTC, BCH, LTC, and BLURT all get amount-jitter too. Per-asset jitter range: up to 999,999 piconero (~$0.0002) for XMR, up to 999 satoshi for BTC/BCH/LTC (~$0.001 to $0.50), up to 99 milliblurt for BLURT (fractions of a cent). The seller is always paid slightly MORE than asked, never less — verification still passes. Default ON; toggle visible right under the amount field in the address-share modal. USDT is excluded: its privacy issue is centralization (Tether can freeze any address), which amount-jitter doesn't address. The per-asset privacy guide at /privacy/{asset} covers each chain's full privacy posture.

feedback_immutable.q: Can feedback be edited or deleted?
feedback_immutable.a:
No, once posted it is permanent. This is what makes reputation meaningful — nobody can quietly erase a bad review. If someone leaves feedback you disagree with, you can post a public response; the original stays.

**If people are going to trust you, your reputation is everything.**

data_collection.q: What data does Morphit collect about me?
data_collection.a: None. Zero cookies. Zero analytics. Zero tracking scripts. No logs of your IP. No third-party services on any Morphit page. We don't know you're here.

lost_keys.q: What if I lose my password or recovery seed?
lost_keys.a: Your account is gone, and we cannot get it back. This is not a mistake — it's the core design. If there were any recovery mechanism, someone would have access to your keys. We refuse to be that someone. Write down your seed on paper.

what_is_blurt.q: Why did Morphit choose the BLURT blockchain?
what_is_blurt.a:
We needed a public **social** blockchain — and that constraint eliminated almost everything else on the market.

Privacy-focused chains like Monero (which we love and trade as a primary asset) are built around hiding amounts, addresses, and metadata. Their users — rightly — refuse to broadcast structured public data because that's antithetical to the whole reason those chains exist. You can't run a public orderbook, immutable reputation system, or auditable trade history on a surveillance-resistant chain; the surveillance resistance is the whole point.

But Morphit's coordination layer needs the opposite: orders, prices, feedback, and order announcements that ANYONE can read and verify, without trusting Morphit. So we needed a chain explicitly designed for public structured data — a SOCIAL chain. After auditing the field (Hive, Steem, Blurt, Lens, Farcaster, ATProto), Blurt won on every metric that mattered:

**1. Three-second block times.** Real-time orderbook updates. New orders confirm in seconds, not minutes — fast enough that high-frequency traders can place and accept orders without lag, and fast enough to **prevent eBay-style last-second sniping**. There's no time window where someone can rush in and grab an order ahead of a buyer who saw it first.

**2. Throughput exceeding Visa + Mastercard combined.** Blurt's witness network can process more transactions per second than every major card network put together. Morphit will never compete with Blurt social-content posts for chain capacity. Listing fees stay tiny because there's no congestion.

**3. Transactions are essentially free.** No mining. No gas auctions. No priority-fee arms races. Posting an order, broadcasting feedback, sending an encrypted chat message — these cost effectively zero in chain fees. Morphit's $0.125 listing fee isn't a chain cost; it's a project decision (anti-Sybil + cover account-creation costs). On a chain like Ethereum or Bitcoin, the fees alone would make a $5 trade impossible.

**4. Built-in end-to-end encrypted chat.** Buyer–seller conversations live on chain as encrypted ciphertexts. Permanent, verifiable, decentralized — and only the two parties hold the keys to read them. Trade-coordination history is durable for posterity (and for any future dispute, you have a courtroom-grade record).

**5. Scammer and spammer prevention.** On-chain identity costs something to create. Posting an order costs something. Sybil tiers escalate fees if you post many orders quickly. Combined with the immutable feedback system, the chain itself is hostile to bad actors. Real traders pay tiny fees; spammers pay rapidly-growing ones.

**6. Immutable public feedback proving reputation.** Every star rating, every comment, every response — permanently recorded, impossible to edit, impossible to delete. **If people are going to trust you, your reputation is everything** — and Blurt makes that reputation provably yours and provably unfakeable.

**7. Fully distributed federated DEX orderbook.** Because the orders live on chain, any operator running their own Morphit indexer sees the SAME orderbook in real-time. There's no central server to attack, no central database to subpoena, no single point of failure. A buyer on instance A sees orders posted through instance B without any cross-server coordination — the chain is the coordination. Multi-site instance runners give the network resilience that no centralized exchange can match.

BLURT is also a social token: holding it gives you posting and voting weight on Blurt content platforms like blurt.blog, blurt.media, and others. So when you pay Morphit listing fees in BLURT, you're not just paying for trade infrastructure — you're directly building stake in a free-speech social network. The loyalty milestones (see the loyalty FAQ) deliberately reward BLURT-paid fees because we want the BLURT economy to thrive alongside Morphit's.

TL;DR: privacy chains can't host public coordination, transparent chains have congestion problems, slow block times kill order matching, and only Blurt combines social-chain design + 3-second blocks + free transactions + social-token economics in one package.

privacy_mode.a: An optional stricter mode that keeps your encrypted keystore in session memory only — it's gone when you close the tab. Use it on shared or public devices. Normal mode keeps your keystore on your own device until you delete it.

use_vpn.q: Can I use a VPN to access Morphit?
use_vpn.a: Yes! In fact, we recommend it. Privacy and security are imperative. Our favorite is Mullvad (mullvad.net) and they accept Monero too!

activity_level.q: How much activity is there on Morphit right now?
activity_level.a:
Live site-wide activity statistics aren't wired up yet. When they ship, this entry will show total successful trades, current active users, and rolled-up activity across every Morphit frontend (morphit.io plus community mirrors). Because the orderbook lives on the Blurt blockchain, those numbers will be verifiable by anyone running their own indexer against the same data.

If you're curious about raw activity right now, you can search the Blurt chain directly for `custom_json` operations with id `morphit_order_v1` — every Morphit order is a signed on-chain op, so anyone can count them without needing our permission or our servers.

sybil_protection.q: How does Morphit stop fake reviews?
sybil_protection.a: Each order costs a small fee, and the fee goes up sharply after a few posts in 24 hours to stop spam. The indexer also spots accounts that look like they're trading with themselves and tags any reviews between them as 'unverified self-trade' — weighted to zero so they don't boost reputation.

no_js.q: Can I use Morphit without JavaScript?
no_js.a: Yes, for browsing. You can read the orderbook, profiles, and feedback with JS off. To trade, JS has to run — because all the cryptography happens inside your browser. If we moved that to a server, we'd have your keys, and that's the one thing we refuse to do.

rss_feeds.q: Can I follow Morphit with RSS?
rss_feeds.a:
Yes, in three forms. Each is a standard RSS 2.0 feed of live, fee-verified orders. Any feed reader can subscribe. No account needed.

**Global feed — `/rss/orderbook.xml`**
The 50 most recent live orders across all assets and traders. Linked from the site footer (the orange RSS pill). Use this when you want to see everything that's posted.

**Per-asset feed — `/rss/orderbook/by-asset/<asset>.xml`**
Filtered to a single asset: `btc.xml`, `xmr.xml`, or `blurt.xml`. Subscribe to only the trades you care about. To find the link, filter the orderbook to the asset you want and look beside the Clear-filters button.

**Per-trader feed — `/rss/orderbook/by-account/@<account>.xml`**
Filtered to a single trader's orders. Subscribe to a counterparty you trust so you're notified the moment they post a new buy or sell order. Find the subscribe link on any trader's profile page beneath their active orders.

**What RSS is good for**: monitoring new orders without keeping a tab open, getting notifications when the main site is slow or blocked in your network, and piping the feed into IFTTT / n8n / a home script for push-notifications the moment something matches.

**Privacy tradeoff — global and per-asset**: Blurt is a public chain, so nothing in these feeds is information a determined observer couldn't already get by running their own chain indexer. But RSS makes that effort drop to zero — anyone polling the feed can build a timeline of who posts when, in which region, for what. The set of valid URLs is small and enumerable (one global + three per-asset), so a passive observer learns at most "this subscriber cares about BTC."

**Privacy tradeoff — per-trader (slightly more revealing)**: A per-trader URL maps one-to-one to one identified subject of interest. A network observer who sees you polling `/rss/orderbook/by-account/@alice.xml` learns specifically that you're watching @alice — slightly more revealing than the global or per-asset feeds. If timing correlation matters in your threat model, poll over Tor.

We ship all three feeds because orderbook transparency is a core Morphit property — and because following a trusted counterparty is something traders genuinely want — not despite the tradeoffs, but with them documented honestly so you can decide what's right for your situation.

why_fresh_addresses.q: Why should I use a new receiving address each time?
why_fresh_addresses.a:
Both Bitcoin and Monero addresses can be watched on the blockchain. If you reuse the same address for every trade, anyone can see all your trades by looking at that one address — how many you've done, roughly when, and how much.

A fresh address each time breaks that link. Your wallet software will happily generate new addresses for free — it's a couple of clicks in any half-decent wallet.

For Monero, Morphit requires a subaddress (the kind that starts with 8, not 4). Subaddresses are Monero's modern privacy default: they look completely unrelated on the blockchain even though they all come from the same wallet. Generate one from your wallet for each trade.

For Bitcoin, we recommend a new address — but we won't block you if you reuse one, you'll just see a reminder. SegWit (bc1…) and Taproot (bc1p…) addresses also pay lower fees and are better for privacy, so prefer those when your wallet gives you the choice.

who_runs_it.a: The project is open-source; the indexer, posting relay, and support bot can all be run by anyone. The morphit.io instance is operated by Agorise, but the whole design assumes morphit.io might go offline — your app keeps working from cache, from mirrors, from Tor, or from Lokinet.

run_your_own.q: Can I run my own Morphit?
run_your_own.a:
Yes, and please do — Morphit only stays unstoppable if lots of people run pieces of it. Here's what you can host:

• A front-end mirror — clone the repo, run one command, and you have a full Morphit at your own domain (or .onion, or .loki). Same code, same orders, your rules about who can reach it. Great for communities that want a curated presence.

• An indexer — watches the Blurt chain, serves the orderbook as REST + RSS, gossips with other indexers. Your indexer's RSS feeds become another path for everyone; your REST API becomes a fallback when others are slow.

• A posting relay — pays the small Blurt network fees so your users don't have to think about them. Run one for your community and make onboarding frictionless.

• A payment watcher, a support bot, or an avatar server — smaller pieces, all useful.

Why it matters: every mirror, every indexer, every relay is an extra path that a censor, a bankrupt host, or a bad court order cannot shut down at once. One instance is a target. Fifty is a movement. Morphit's core promise — non-custodial, no-KYC, uncensorable — only holds as long as enough people are willing to run a copy. If you have a VPS, a Raspberry Pi, a spare laptop, or even a mid-range phone, you can contribute. All the services are single-binary Go programs with plain config files; the README walks you through it in minutes, not hours.

The more people who run Morphit, the harder it is for anyone to take it away from the rest of us.

security_attack_vectors.q: Is Morphit vulnerable to hacking, data theft, or takedowns?
security_attack_vectors.a: The best defense is the design itself. Morphit is non-custodial — your Blurt private keys never leave your device and are never transmitted to our servers, so there is no key database for anyone to steal. There are no accounts, no passwords, no sessions, and no login state, which means no credential phishing, no session hijacking, and no account-takeover class of attack. We do not collect KYC and we do not log IPs, so there is no personal-information database that could be breached or subpoenaed. The orderbook lives on the Blurt blockchain itself — any user can run their own indexer and their own frontend — so censorship and takedowns cannot delete orders, only hide them from one particular mirror. Standard web attack surfaces (XSS, CSRF, SSRF, RCE, SQL injection, parameter pollution) are addressed through a combination of strict Content Security Policy headers, exact-origin CORS allowlists, schema-validated request bodies with bounded field lengths, no eval / no dynamic code paths, no server-side database queries on user input, and a relay service that only speaks to pre-configured Blurt RPC endpoints. We also have no PHP, no WordPress, no xmlrpc.php, and no OAuth layer, so entire vulnerability classes that plague other platforms simply do not apply here. Volumetric (network-level) DDoS is beyond the reach of any application to solve alone — that belongs to the VPS provider or an upstream scrubbing service — but application-layer abuse is mitigated by per-IP rate limits, 64 KiB request body caps, and tight resource ceilings. The full threat model is documented in SECURITY.md and ADR-0006 in the project repository.

security_engineering_rigor.q: How rigorous is Morphit's security review process?
security_engineering_rigor.a:
Very. Security on Morphit isn't a marketing claim — it's a sustained engineering practice with a documented audit trail anyone can read.

**The audit lives in the repository.** `docs/AUDIT-2026-05.md` in the public source tree is a running document of every security review pass we've done on the codebase, organized by date and subsystem. It's not a one-time pre-launch certificate; it's a working log that gets a new entry every time we audit a meaningful change. Every finding is given a severity rating, a description, and an outcome — fixed inline, deferred to a tracked follow-up, or accepted with rationale. Items we choose not to fix immediately go into `docs/REVISIT-LIST.md` (also public) with full context so nothing falls through the cracks.

**We use formal threat-modeling methodology.** Each audit pass runs a STRIDE matrix (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) over every changed subsystem, then builds attack trees from the most attractive entry points, then writes adversarial red-team narratives walking through what a determined attacker — we name them and give them goals — would actually do. This is the same methodology used in commercial security reviews; the difference is we publish the result.

**Open source means open audit.** Morphit is AGPL-3.0. The full source code is at git.agorise.net/agorise/morphit. Anyone can clone the repo, read the code, run the test suite (over 1,000 self-checks ship with the source), submit issues, and propose patches. We treat external review as an asset, not a threat. The threat model assumes a sophisticated attacker has already read every line of code — because that's the realistic worst case, and designing for it is what makes the system actually safe.

**Privacy-first defaults.** The architecture is built so that even a complete server compromise doesn't leak much, because we deliberately don't have much to leak. No KYC. No email. No phone number. No IP retention. No central key store. No session cookies. Chat is end-to-end encrypted; the indexer stores only ciphertext and could not decrypt your conversations even under legal compulsion. Trade verification for cryptocurrencies happens on the user's own device against the user's own node — Morphit never sees your view keys, your wallet, or your funds. The threat model treats every operator as untrusted by default; the federation lets users choose whose mirror to use, and switch at any time.

**Monero users in particular**: we know your community is the most rigorous in crypto about privacy. Every Monero-related change goes through extra scrutiny because the cost of a privacy mistake on XMR is permanent. The marketplace never holds your XMR, never asks for view keys, never proxies your transactions, never logs your IP, and never sees your wallet. Where a naive marketplace would expose linkable amounts on chain, Morphit's order math includes amount-randomization features specifically designed to defeat the obvious correlation attack. We've shipped multiple rounds of work specifically to harden Monero flows; the testing suite covers the cases we expect adversaries to try.

**Discipline beats heroics.** The single most important security property of any system is whether the team treats issues as systemic engineering work or as embarrassments to be downplayed. Morphit is run as the former. When we ship a feature, we audit it; when we audit it, we publish what we found; when we find something, we fix it or document why we didn't. The audit document and the revisit list together total many thousands of lines and grow steadily. Some of what's in there is unflattering — that's the point. A security review that finds nothing isn't a thorough review; it's a shallow one.

**What we deliberately don't publish.** We do publish our defensive-economics math (the cost to attempt various Sybil attacks is openly documented, because deterrence works best when attackers can see the math is against them). We don't publish exact internal heuristics, rate-limit thresholds, or detection signal weights, because those would give an evasion roadmap to an attacker without correspondingly helping defenders. The ratio of public to private information is calibrated to maximize attacker friction while letting honest users verify our work.

**Bug bounty program.** We run a discretionary security recognition program. Every actionable finding gets reviewed by a real engineer, gets an answer, and — if it materially improves Morphit's security posture — gets rewarded in BLURT (paid from @morphit-fees) or BTC, scaled to severity and the report's quality. No fixed tier table; case-by-case adjudication. Hall of fame credit available even when payment isn't. Send a Matrix DM to **@agorise:matrix.org** for confidential disclosure (end-to-end encrypted by default), or open a confidential issue on git.agorise.net. Full scope, severity guidance, and payment workflow at /security#bounty and in `docs/SECURITY.md`.

If you're evaluating Morphit and you want to verify any of the above for yourself: clone the repo and read `docs/AUDIT-2026-05.md`, `docs/REVISIT-LIST.md`, `SECURITY.md`, and the ADR series. Everything is there.

help_make_unstoppable.q: How can I help make Morphit unstoppable?
help_make_unstoppable.a:
Morphit's resilience grows with every independent operator. You can help in any of these ways:

• Run your own node. Spin up an indexer + relay + frontend on your own server (or VPS, or home box), and serve Morphit from your own URL. Every independent mirror multiplies our surface area: blocking one does nothing when ten more exist. See the 'Can I run my own Morphit?' entry for the technical steps.

• Host on Tor, Lokinet, or I2P. A .onion, .loki, or .b32.i2p mirror lets users reach Morphit from jurisdictions where clearnet access is blocked. These are cheap to run — they don't need TLS certificates or DNS — and the impact is enormous for users in censored networks.

• Host Morphit's dependencies. The frontend pulls a handful of JavaScript libraries at build time. Self-hosting mirrors of those packages (or proxying their CDNs) lets communities bootstrap without relying on third parties. We'll document the exact list in the operator runbook.

• Fund a community node. If you don't want to run servers yourself, contributing BLURT to an active operator's @morphit-relay account keeps their account-creation tokens topped up. One operator covering 500 weekly signups needs ~$1 of BLURT per week; small contributions add up.

• Spread the word. Morphit depends on network effect — every user who posts a trade is a signal to the next person that the marketplace is alive. Tell your crypto communities, link us from your blog, post tutorials on blurt.media.

• Write tutorials and translations. The project is AGPL-3.0; clone the repo, improve documentation, translate the UI into more languages, and open a merge request. Non-code contributions count.

Morphit is designed to be impossible to kill because there is no central actor to pressure. You running ANY part of the stack makes that guarantee stronger.

why_self_trading_fails.q: Why doesn't trading with myself work to boost my reputation?
why_self_trading_fails.a:
Self-trading is economically unprofitable on Morphit by design.

Here's the math: each listing costs about $0.25 to post (the fee goes to @morphit-fees, not to your counterparty). If you post a buy order and a sell order with two accounts you control, you pay $0.50 for the round trip. Each 'successful trade' produces one feedback entry you can sign to yourself. Cost per fake feedback: $0.50.

Now consider detection. Morphit's indexer runs signal analysis that flags suspicious reciprocity — accounts that trade exclusively with each other, accounts created within minutes of each other, and accounts sharing an account-creator relationship. Those signals are PUBLIC on every order row. A reputation built entirely from self-trades shows the signal badge; real traders avoid you; you've spent your fake-reputation money for nothing.

Even the Sybil fee tier is stacked against this abuse. Your 4th order in 24 hours pays 1.25× the base fee; your 5th pays 1.56×; your 10th pays 4.77×. Running a fake-reputation factory at any useful speed gets expensive fast.

The honest path is cheaper, faster, and actually works: post good orders, communicate clearly with counterparties, show up with payment promptly. Feedback from real traders looks different from self-trading feedback — timing distribution, counterparty variety, geographic spread. The people checking your reputation can tell.

why_multi_accounts_fail.q: Can I register many accounts through Morphit to spam the orderbook?
why_multi_accounts_fail.a:
You can — but the economics make it unprofitable, and the system is designed to stay that way.

Each Morphit relay pre-mints Account Creation Tokens (ACTs) at ~100 BLURT each in a weekly batch ceremony, and consumes one ACT per signup. So every account a Morphit relay creates costs the operator ~$0.20 of pre-paid token. To recover this, Morphit requires a listing fee on every order you post after your first. An attacker registering bulk accounts and never posting wastes ~$0.20 per account of Morphit's BLURT — so we rate-limit signups to 2 per IP per day at the network layer, and the relay's pre-minted ACT pool size caps the total damage to one week's worth of signup capacity (operators mint ~25 ACTs/week by default). An attacker who wants to exceed our rate limits has to rotate IPs (which is non-trivial and expensive at scale); the rate limit is an annoyance for abusers and invisible to normal users.

If you register accounts AND post orders to spam the orderbook, each order pays its $0.25 listing fee. 100 spam orders = $25 of your real money. Meanwhile Morphit's indexer flags related-account patterns automatically and shows that signal publicly on the orderbook, so your spam is conspicuous.

The welcome bonus (10 BLURT + 10 BLURT Power) is delayed until AFTER your first successful trade is confirmed by counterparty feedback — so you cannot collect welcome bonuses at scale without also completing real trades with real counterparties. A farmer who fakes trades between their own accounts pays the listing fees and gets flagged by signal analysis; they never net a profit.

We publish these mechanics openly because deterrence works best when attackers can see the math. It's always cheaper to be a real trader than a fake one on Morphit.

blurt_benefits.q: What is BLURT and why does Morphit sometimes mention it?
blurt_benefits.a:
Morphit settles its on-chain coordination on a public ledger called Blurt. The ledger's native unit is also called BLURT — every block, every signature, every fee transfer flows through it. You can think of BLURT as the gas token for the coordination layer, the same way ETH is gas for Ethereum, but smaller and quieter.

You don't have to interact with BLURT to trade BTC or XMR on Morphit. If your operator accepts BTC or XMR for the network fee (most do), you can list orders, message counterparties, and complete trades without ever touching BLURT.

Why does it come up at all? Three reasons:

1. **Network fees can be paid in BLURT** as an alternative to BTC/XMR. Some users prefer this because BLURT confirmations are instant — no waiting for external block explorers. If your operator has only BLURT configured for fees, this is the path you'll use.

2. **The welcome bonus is denominated in BLURT** (a small one-time gift after your first successful trade). It's harmless to ignore, or you can spend it on future network fees.

3. **Your BLURT balance gives you voting weight** on Blurt-social frontends like blurt.blog. That's outside Morphit's scope but if you find yourself with BLURT and curious, those are your options.

Morphit is built on Blurt because the ledger's design (low transaction overhead, free posts, public-by-default state) fits a peer-to-peer trade venue better than the alternatives we evaluated. We treat the ledger as plumbing — necessary, deliberately chosen, but not something you should have to think about while trading.

where_to_buy_blurt.q: Where do I buy BLURT to use as a network fee?
where_to_buy_blurt.a:
**Buy it on Morphit itself — that's the whole point.** Morphit is a peer-to-peer marketplace; BLURT is one of the six assets traded here, alongside BTC, XMR, USDT, BCH, and LTC. Visit /orderbook, filter for BLURT sell orders, and message a counterparty. You pay them in whatever fiat or method they accept; they send BLURT to your Blurt account. Done.

**Your first order is free.** New users get a one-time waiver that covers the listing fee on their first BLURT buy — see "Is my first order really free?" for details. So your first BLURT acquisition can also be your first trade on Morphit, with no exchange account, no card, and no KYC required. The waiver is offered automatically when you compose your first order.

**Last-resort alternative:** if you genuinely cannot find a counterparty on the Morphit orderbook (the orderbook is small in some regions), Klingex.io runs a BLURT/USDT trading pair as a centralized-exchange fallback. We mention it for completeness but treat it as an emergency option — every BLURT bought through Klingex is a trade Morphit didn't get, and the goal of the project is to grow the peer-to-peer orderbook, not to send users off-site. If you do go this route, the trade page is at https://klingex.io/trade/BLURT-USDT and you'll need to deposit USDT to swap into BLURT. Withdraw to your own Blurt wallet immediately rather than leaving funds on the exchange.

**Once you have BLURT in your wallet**, paying a Morphit listing fee is automatic — choose "Pay in BLURT" on the post-order screen and Morphit deducts the configured fee directly from your Blurt balance with no extra steps.

first_order_free.q: Is my first order really free?
first_order_free.a:
Yes — and it's a really generous one. Your first order on Morphit is a free buy of at least 500 BLURT (≈$1). We cover the listing fee. One free order per account, for life.

**Why BLURT specifically, and not BTC or XMR?** Because the BLURT in your wallet is what makes you an active participant in everything else on Morphit. With 500+ BLURT, you can:

- Pay listing fees on ~8 future orders at the discounted BLURT rate (60 BLURT each — 50% off the BTC/XMR rate)
- Vote on Blurt social content at blurt.blog, blurt.media, etc. and earn curation rewards
- Receive a 1 BP delegation as your welcome stake (fires automatically on your first BLURT-paid listing fee)
- After your first completed trade, receive 10 BLURT liquid + 10 BLURT Power as the welcome bonus

Without the BLURT in your wallet, you'd start with no way to pay future listing fees at the discount, no Blurt voting weight, and no path into the loyalty-milestone reward tiers. We thought a long time about this — handing new users some BLURT instead of "any first crypto" sets you up to be active rather than stranded.

**Why a 500 BLURT minimum?** That's the threshold that makes the rest of the math work: enough to cover ~8 future listings at the discounted rate. If we let the waiver apply to a tiny 1-BLURT buy, you'd leave the flow with effectively no starter balance and the bonus wouldn't help you. 500 BLURT (~$1 at typical recent prices) is the minimum that turns the waiver into a meaningful starter pack.

**The waiver is offered automatically** when you visit /post and start composing your first order. The Review step shows a green "🌱 First order is free" panel with the waiver pre-selected. You can decline if you'd rather save the waiver for a future trade — it never expires.

**What "free" means here:** Morphit covers the listing fee for this one order. You don't pay any network fee. The trade itself happens off-platform between you and your counterparty (they send you BLURT, you pay them whatever fiat or other thing you agreed on); Morphit doesn't touch your funds at any point.

**After your first trade:** the waiver is consumed and the normal fee structure applies — $0.25 in BTC/XMR or $0.125 in BLURT (the 50% BLURT discount is permanent). See "What are the fees?" for the full pricing.

welcome_bonus.q: What is the welcome bonus and how do I earn it?
welcome_bonus.a:
There are actually three welcome rewards on Morphit, and they fire at different moments:

**1. First listing-fee payment in BLURT → 1 BP delegated.** The moment you pay your first BLURT listing fee — even before any trade matches or completes — Morphit delegates 1 BP (Blurt Power) to your account. This is a tiny, one-time "welcome to the network" stake that starts earning APR/curation rewards immediately. It fires regardless of whether your order eventually finds a counterparty. Once-per-account.

**2. First completed trade → 10 BLURT liquid + 10 BLURT Power.** When you complete your first actual trade (counterparty signs feedback citing the order), Morphit sends you 10 BLURT liquid plus 10 BLURT Power (≈13 BP of voting weight). "Completed" means: you posted an order, a counterparty responded, the trade settled off-platform, and the counterparty signed positive feedback about you that cites your order. That feedback is what triggers this bonus — it's proof of a real trade with another human, not just a posted-and-abandoned order.

**3. Loyalty milestones → up to 1,260 BP.** As you pay more BLURT fees over time, you cross 100/500/2,000/10,000 BLURT thresholds and receive delegation increases (10/50/200/1,000 BP at each tier). See the loyalty FAQ for details.

Why the staggered design: handing out the full bonus at signup would be farmed by Sybil accounts in minutes. The 1 BP welcome on first paid fee is a small enough amount that Sybil farming is unprofitable ($0.125 cost per attacker per 1 BP), and the larger 10 BLURT liquid + 10 BLURT Power requires real trade evidence (counterparty feedback). Both add up to meaningful staking weight for honest users.

If you trade exclusively in BTC or XMR and never pay a BLURT listing fee, you'll receive the 10 BLURT liquid + 10 BLURT Power from your first completed trade but not the 1 BP first-fee welcome (which is BLURT-fee-gated). The BLURT bonus is harmless to receive and ignore — it can sit in your account indefinitely or cover future network fees.

The rewards arrive as `delegate_vesting_shares` and `transfer` ops from @morphit-relay in your account history.

loyalty_milestones.q: How do loyalty rewards work? (The BP milestones I saw mentioned)
loyalty_milestones.a:
Every time you pay a listing fee in BLURT, your cumulative lifetime spending with Morphit is tracked. When you cross certain thresholds, Morphit sends you a Blurt Power (BP) delegation as a thank-you. Four tiers:

• 100 BLURT paid cumulatively → 10 BP delegated
• 500 BLURT paid cumulatively → 50 BP delegated  
• 2,000 BLURT paid cumulatively → 200 BP delegated
• 10,000 BLURT paid cumulatively → 1,000 BP delegated

The thresholds measure cumulative lifetime BLURT fees paid — they don't reset, and they don't require the fees to be recent. If you pay 100 BLURT of fees over two years of trading, you still get the 10 BP reward the moment you cross the threshold.

BP (Blurt Power) gives you voting weight on Blurt content across blurt.blog, blurt.media, and any other Blurt frontend. It's a "you matter more in this network" stake. You don't spend it by voting; your voting weight refills over time. And votes you cast can earn you curation rewards when you vote early on content that later becomes popular.

Important mechanics to know:
• The milestones only count fees paid in BLURT. BTC/XMR fees and waived-first-buy orders don't count toward the thresholds. This is deliberate — the loyalty program exists to reward users who support the BLURT economy.
• The reward is a DELEGATION, not a transfer. Morphit delegates BP to your account, and retains the ability to undelegate if the account is later found to be engaged in abuse (fake trades, sybil attacks). For honest users this never matters.
• Each tier fires once per account. If you cross 100 BLURT, then later 500, you get 10 BP + 50 BP = 60 BP total delegated. Not "the bigger tier replaces the smaller" — they add up.
• You see the milestone arrive as a delegate_vesting_shares op from @morphit-relay in your account history. It shows up in Blurt wallet UIs as incoming BP.

These four loyalty tiers stack on top of two earlier welcome rewards: the **1 BP delegation** you receive on your first BLURT-paid listing fee, and the **10 BLURT liquid + 10 BLURT Power** you receive after your first completed trade. Together, an active trader can accumulate up to 1,261 BP in total delegations over their Morphit lifetime, all of which translates directly into voting weight in the wider Blurt social network. See the welcome-bonus FAQ for the full three-tier reward system.

no_escrow_arbitration.q: Why no Escrow or Arbitration service?
no_escrow_arbitration.a:
Escrow is a babysitter who holds your money until the trade finishes. If you and the other kid argue, the arbitrator is the referee who decides who gets the toys.

The risk:
You stopped trusting the other person… and now you have to trust the babysitter AND the referee instead. Both are centralizing — they become the new middleman with power over your money. If they're dishonest, slow, biased, or get hacked, your money can still disappear.

Bottom line:
Escrow + arbitration just moves the trust problem to a different person/group.

Don't trust. Verify.

no_js_limits.q: What does the 'No JS' link in the footer do?
no_js_limits.a:
Right now: nothing functional — it's a placeholder pointing here, to explain the state.

What it will do: load the site with no JavaScript boot script, so nothing runs in your browser beyond what the server sent. Browsing (orderbook, FAQ, profiles) already works this way — the pages are statically rendered, and you can verify this by disabling JS in your browser and reloading. What JavaScript adds is the interactive layer: placing orders, decrypting chat, signing feedback, switching languages without a page reload.

Why it isn't wired up yet: Morphit currently ships every page as prerendered HTML plus a hydration script. A per-request `?nojs=1` switch that suppresses hydration needs an architectural change (per-request SSR instead of prerender + hydrate) that's on the roadmap but not yet built. In the meantime, disabling JS in your browser's own settings gets you the same outcome — the static HTML is already there.

So: browsing without JS already works today; turn it off in your browser if you want to confirm. The pill becomes functional once per-request SSR ships.

how_to_run_node.q: How do I run a Morphit node?
how_to_run_node.a:
