This pattern matches the typical sock-puppet farm setup where one operator creates multiple accounts via blurt-cli and immediately starts using them. Real users who happen to share a creator (a friend who helped onboard them via blurt-cli) and start using Morphit minutes apart can occasionally trip this — operator-side appeal is possible.

2. **Mutual high-star with no third party.** Two accounts that exchange 3+ five-star reviews of each other in 7 days AND have not reviewed any third party in that window. This pattern matches a sock-puppet farm doing wash trades to inflate ratings. Real heavy-traders almost always have third-party reviews mixed in, so this rarely false-positives on legitimate users. If you have been flagged and you are a real user, complete a few trades with different counterparties — the rolling 7-day window will let the flag fall off naturally next time the detector runs.

**Why we flag rather than hide:** the reviews stay visible because the chain itself is public — anyone running their own indexer can see them. Hiding them in this UI would be cosmetic only, and it would be dishonest about what the reputation system is actually doing. The chip + reduced opacity convey "this exists but does not count" clearly while preserving transparency.

**Why headline excludes them:** the rating + count at the top of the profile is the at-a-glance trust signal traders use to decide whether to engage. Including suppressed reviews in that number would defeat the purpose of detecting them. The list view is for due-diligence reading; the headline is for snap judgments.

**False positives:** the detectors are not perfect. If you believe you have been wrongly flagged, the operator running the indexer instance you are looking at can manually unflag a pair — open a thread on the project discussion forum or contact the instance operator.

See also "How does Morphit reputation system work?" for the bigger picture.

block_privacy.q: If I block someone, will they know?
block_privacy.a:
**Morphit does not show blocked users that they have been blocked.** This is a deliberate anti-harassment design choice, not a privacy guarantee.

When you block someone, what happens:

- The block decision is broadcast on the Blurt chain as a `morphit_block_v1` op. This is technically public — anyone scraping the chain can see "@you blocked @them on date X."
- Morphit's interface deliberately does not surface "you have been blocked by @x" anywhere. The blocked user can still try to send messages to you, but those messages do not land on your end and they get no error indication telling them they have been blocked specifically. From their side, it just looks like delivery failed.
- This is the standard anti-harassment posture used by most social platforms. Telling a stalker exactly which account is blocking them helps them figure out how to evade the block. Telling nobody preserves the victim's safety.

What this means in practice:

- If you block someone and they retry sending, their message is silently rejected. They do not get a popup saying "you are blocked." They might assume the indexer is having trouble or they typed the wrong account.
- If they try to message you from a different account, that new account hits the layer-2 stranger-fee gate ($0.01 minimum, escalating if they keep trying fast) AND the layer-3 fan-in cap (maximum 20 new strangers per 24h on your inbox). So even creating new accounts to evade your block costs them real money and is bounded.
- A determined stalker who scrapes the Blurt chain directly can find your block decision. There is no realistic way to hide this — the chain is public. But Morphit's UI does not make it convenient for them.

If you change your mind, you can unblock someone via Settings → Blocked Accounts. Unblocking is also broadcast on-chain (so other Morphit instances see the change), but it does not retroactively deliver messages they tried to send while blocked.

See also "How does Morphit stop spam and unsolicited messages from strangers?" for the broader anti-spam design.

what_is_mana.a:
On Blurt, Mana is the per-account capacity that lets you do things on the chain — post, comment, vote, and (in Morphit's case) submit orders, broadcast feedback, send chat messages.

Think of Mana like a video-game stamina bar that refills on its own. Every action you take spends a little. The bar slowly recharges over the next few hours and days. If you're a normal user, you'll basically never notice it — Blurt's design refills Mana fast enough that you can do dozens of things per day without thinking about it.

Mana is the answer to the spam question: "if posting on a blockchain is free, why doesn't everyone just spam?" Because spamming would burn through your Mana bar in seconds, and then you'd have to wait it out while everyone else's actions go through normally. Blurt's economy uses this to throttle abuse without anyone needing to charge fees on each post.

The size of your Mana bar is roughly proportional to how much BLURT you're holding (specifically, BLURT Power — staked BLURT). New accounts get a small starter amount, which is why the welcome bonus includes some BLURT Power: it bumps up your bar so you can use Morphit smoothly from day one.

**Note on terminology.** You may see this called "RC" or "Resource Credits" in older Blurt documentation, on the Steem network it forked from, or in our internal code comments. Mana is the modern Blurt name, and what we use everywhere a normal user can see.

node_minimum_requirements.q: What are the minimum hardware requirements to run a Morphit node?
node_minimum_requirements.a:
Surprisingly modest.  Morphit is built to run on hardware most people already own.  Three categories of setups people are using:

**Hobbyist tier — Raspberry Pi 4 / 5 (4 GB).**  Runs the indexer, relay, and frontend together comfortably.  Use a USB-3 SSD instead of an SD card; SD cards die under database write load.  Power draw is around 5–7 W, so a small UPS or solar setup handles it for hours.  Suitable for serving a personal community of a few dozen active users.

**Serious tier — small mini-PC (Beelink, Intel NUC, generic 2nd-hand).**  An Intel N100 / Ryzen 3xxx with 8 GB RAM and any modern SSD is overkill for the indexer and runs every Morphit service at the same time without thinking about it.  Power draw 6–10 W idle, 15–20 W under load.  $150–250 used.  Comfortable for an instance serving hundreds of active users.

**Spare-laptop tier — anything that still boots Linux.**  An old ThinkPad or any laptop from the last decade with at least 4 GB RAM and a working SSD is plenty.  Bonus: built-in UPS (the laptop battery).  Some operators leave a closed laptop on a shelf running Morphit on a wired Ethernet connection — works great.

**Concrete minimums (any architecture: x86-64, ARM64, or Apple silicon under Asahi):**

• **CPU:** 2 cores at 1 GHz or faster.  Indexer is mostly I/O-bound; relay is mostly idle.  No GPU needed, ever.

• **RAM:** 2 GB minimum, 4 GB comfortable.  Postgres fits inside that with the default config; tuning Postgres `shared_buffers` to 256 MB on a 2 GB system avoids paging.

• **Disk:** 20 GB free, on an SSD.  HDDs technically work but Postgres will be slow and SD cards will die from write amplification.  The indexer's database grows slowly — measured in low-MB per month for typical activity — so 20 GB lasts years.  Plan for backups, though.

• **Network:** 1 Mbit/s up and down is enough.  An average page load is around 100 KB.  A small instance serving a few users uses a few GB of bandwidth a month, well within any home internet cap.  Static IP is nice but not required — dynamic-DNS works fine.

• **Operating system:** Any modern Linux (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04+, Arch, Alpine, NixOS — we test on Debian).  FreeBSD works with minor adjustments.  macOS works for development but isn't recommended for a public instance.

• **Uptime expectation:** 95% is a reasonable target.  Morphit is federated by design — when your instance is down, users fall back to other operators' instances and back to you when you return.  The chain holds the data; your instance is just one of many windows into it.

**What you do NOT need:**

• A Blurt blockchain node.  Morphit talks to public Blurt RPC endpoints over HTTPS.

• A static IP.  Use Caddy or Cloudflare Tunnel (or, for this project's privacy values, a reverse proxy plus DDNS) to expose port 443.  See the operator handbook for non-Cloudflare options.

• A domain name.  You can run a private instance on `https://morphit.local` for your friends, or expose a `.onion` / `.loki` / `.b32.i2p` address only.

• A datacenter VPS.  Operators running on residential connections work fine, especially with alt-network reachability so users don't need your home IP.

The operator-earnings split is sized so that even a Pi-tier instance covers its hosting cost and your time at modest activity levels.  Run one because you want a Morphit that exists in your community, not because it pays well — but the math doesn't lose money.

iphone_install.q: Can I use Morphit on my iPhone without jailbreaking?
iphone_install.a:
Yes — fully, without jailbreaking. Here's the honest situation:

**Why no native App Store app.** Apple's App Store guidelines reject apps that facilitate non-KYC peer-to-peer cryptocurrency exchange. Morphit's whole design — non-custodial, no identity verification, federated across operators — is exactly what they refuse to publish. So we don't pretend to have a native iOS app; we'd be lying if we did.

**What works perfectly: Progressive Web App (PWA) install.** Modern Safari supports installing websites as standalone apps. The icon goes on your Home Screen, the app launches fullscreen (no Safari URL bar), service workers cache assets for offline browsing, and the app remembers state between launches.

**The install flow** (takes about 15 seconds):
1. Open this site in Safari. Not Chrome or Firefox — those use Safari's web engine on iOS but don't expose the PWA install path.
2. Tap the Share icon at the bottom of the screen (a square with an up-arrow).
3. Scroll down in the share sheet and tap "Add to Home Screen."
4. Confirm the name ("Morphit" by default) and tap "Add" in the top-right.

Done. The icon is on your Home Screen alongside your other apps. Tap to launch fullscreen.

**iOS version notes.** iOS 16.4+ has full PWA support: service workers (offline caching), push notifications, badge counts, Web Share Target. Older iOS versions still install — the icon works, the site loads — but without those advanced features. iOS 14-16.3 launches the PWA fullscreen but won't cache for offline use.

**Comparison to Android.** Android users have more options: install our APK directly, install through F-Droid / Aptoide / APKPure, install through GrapheneOS (without Google Play). iOS only offers the PWA path because of Apple's stricter ecosystem. The PWA experience itself is comparable to a native app for Morphit's use case — you're trading, chatting, and reading the orderbook, all of which are HTTP-and-crypto operations that don't benefit from native APIs.

**TestFlight.** We don't currently distribute via TestFlight (Apple's developer beta tool). Reasons: the 90-day expiration on TestFlight builds means we'd be re-distributing on a schedule, the 10,000-tester cap doesn't fit a public app, and the same App Store guidelines apply to TestFlight reviews as to public store listings — Apple would still reject a non-KYC P2P crypto app. The PWA path is the lasting answer.

**Sideloading via AltStore / etc.** AltStore lets developers sideload IPA files using a free Apple Developer account. It works but requires the user to re-sign the app every 7 days (Apple's free developer cert expires). For a security-sensitive app like Morphit, requiring users to weekly re-sign creates an attack window where a malicious update could be slipped in. The PWA install is one-tap, free, and doesn't expire.

**Bottom line for grandma:** Open Morphit in Safari on your iPhone. Tap Share, then "Add to Home Screen." Done. Your iPhone treats Morphit like an app from then on.

block_explorer.q: Is there a block explorer for Morphit?
block_explorer.a: Yes — visit /explorer to look up any Blurt account, transaction, or block. The explorer is public and works without an account. Completed trades on Morphit are visible there with rich Morphit-aware decoration on each operation. For BTC and XMR transactions, Morphit links out to the appropriate external explorer (mempool.space for Bitcoin, xmrchain.net for Monero).

public_api.q: Can I build a block explorer or aggregator on top of Morphit's data?
public_api.a:
**Yes — this is supported, encouraged, and free.**

Every Morphit instance exposes a documented public HTTP API at `/v1/*`.  Same contract on every operator's box — different hostname, identical shape.  The endpoints are read-only, no authentication required, no API key, no signup.  Just hit the URL.

**Documented contract.** The full reference is at `docs/API.md` in the source repo.  Endpoints we promise stable shape for: `/v1/orderbook`, `/v1/orderbook/stream` (SSE), `/v1/orderbook/featured`, `/v1/orders/:account`, `/v1/accounts/:account`, `/v1/accounts/:account/feedback`, `/v1/accounts/:account/feedback-given`, `/v1/instances`, `/v1/instances/stream`, `/v1/operators`, `/v1/health`, `/v1/instance`, `/v1/listing-fee`, `/v1/chain-fee`, `/v1/release`, plus three RSS endpoints (`/rss/orderbook.xml`, `/rss/orderbook/by-asset/*`, `/rss/orderbook/by-account/*`).

**Response shapes are versioned.** Anything documented under `/v1/*` won't have fields renamed or removed without a `/v2/*` version bump.  Adding new fields is non-breaking and you should ignore unknown fields.  Versioning policy in detail at `docs/API.md`.

**Rate limits.** 120 req/min for list endpoints, 600 req/min for single-record lookups, per-IP per-minute, operator-tunable.  If you need higher throughput, run your own indexer — see `RUN-A-MORPHIT-NODE.md`.  Self-hosting gives you no rate limits and faster response times for your application.

**Why this design makes sense.** Morphit's whole architecture is built on the idea that data lives on the public Blurt chain and any indexer can recompute it.  A locked-down API would be security theater because the underlying chain ops are already public — anyone scraping Blurt directly can build their own Morphit indexer in a weekend.  Documenting the existing endpoints just makes the same data accessible to people who don't want to build their own chain indexer first.

**What CAN'T you do via this API:**

- Write data.  Writes happen via signed `custom_json` ops broadcast to a Blurt RPC node.  See `apps/web/src/lib/blurt/sign.ts` for the pattern.
- Read encrypted chat content.  Chat ciphertext is on-chain (visible to anyone) but only the two participants have the keys.
- Read private order metrics (e.g. per-order viewcount is gated to the order owner).
- Bypass the operator's rate limits.  Run your own instance instead.

**Examples of what people build with this:**

- **Block explorers** that decorate Morphit ops on top of generic Blurt explorers
- **Federation health monitors** scraping `/v1/instances` for instance status
- **Trading-bot price feeds** combining `/v1/orderbook` data with external BLURT/USD prices
- **CLI clients** for sysadmins who want a terminal interface to Morphit
- **Academic research** on P2P market dynamics, Sybil-resistance economics, and federated reputation systems
- **Mobile apps** by operators or third parties who want a native experience while respecting Morphit's federation
- **RSS-driven dashboards** for traders who want order-feed alerts in their existing news reader

If you're building something interesting on the API, drop a note on the operators' Matrix channel — we'll add your project to a curated list of API consumers and link it from the operator handbook.

**Self-hosting as a first-class path.** If your aggregator is going to be high-volume, the right answer is run your own indexer.  ~$5/month VPS, 30-minute setup (see `RUN-A-MORPHIT-NODE.md`), full speed-of-light access to the data.  No rate limits, no operator-availability dependency, no aggregator-vs-instance fragility.  This is the path serious projects should take.

what_is_featured_slot.q: What is the featured slot and how does the auction work?
what_is_featured_slot.a:
Featured slots are the top **5 highest-paying** orders that appear at the top of the orderbook page in a special highlighted section.  They get more visibility than the regular orderbook list — useful when you want a fast trade and are willing to pay a small fee to be seen first.

**How bidding works.** You bid by paying BLURT into the Morphit fee account along with a `morphit_feature_bid_v1` op naming your order and the number of hours you want featured time.  The rate you pay (BLURT per hour) determines your rank: the 5 highest-rate active bids are visible at any moment.

**Bid rules:**
• **Minimum bid duration:** 6 hours.  Prevents one-hour cheap-shots from displacing serious multi-day bidders.
• **Maximum bid duration:** 1 week (168 hours) per bid.
• **Min-bid increment:** if your bid would displace someone currently visible, you must beat them by at least `max(1 BLURT/hour, 5%)`.  Prevents penny-war bidding spam.

**What you pay:** rate × hours, in BLURT, transferred to the Morphit fee account when you submit the bid.  The fee is non-refundable — see the **What happens if I get outbid?** entry for what "non-refundable" means in practice.

**Who sees featured slots:** every visitor to the orderbook page on every Morphit instance.  Featured-slot rendering is part of the standard orderbook view, not opt-in.

featured_slot_displaced.q: What happens to my featured slot if someone outbids me?
featured_slot_displaced.a:
Your bid stays alive — you don't lose your money — but you lose visibility until the higher bidder's slot ends or you're un-displaced.

**Concretely:** Morphit shows the top 5 highest-paying active bids.  If a 6th bidder posts a meaningfully higher rate (max of 1 BLURT/hour or 5% above the current 5th-place bid — small increments are rejected to prevent grief-displacement), you drop to position 6 and become invisible in the featured section.  Your bid record stays in the indexer.  When any of the bids above you expires (their hours run out), you bubble up.  If you eventually rise back into the top 5 before your own hours expire, you become visible again.

**No refund for displaced minutes.** This is deliberate.  Refunds would require re-broadcasting transfer ops on every displacement — operationally messy and would create a perverse incentive (bid high, get displaced, get refunded, repeat).  The simple rule is: you paid for N hours of *eligibility for the featured slot*, not N hours of *guaranteed visibility*.

**How to avoid being displaced:**
• Watch the current top-5 rates before bidding.  If the lowest visible rate is 10 BLURT/hour, bidding 8 BLURT/hour means you're queued, not visible.
• Bid for shorter durations.  6 hours of guaranteed-visible time is often more useful than 24 hours of "might get displaced midway."
• Bid during low-traffic times.  Featured-slot competition is higher when more traders are posting.

**Two protections built into the platform:**

• **Outbid push notifications.**  If you've subscribed to Web Push (Settings → Notifications), Morphit sends a notification the moment you drop out of the top 5, with a deep-link to the affected order in `/my/orders`.  You'll know within seconds — you don't have to refresh the orderbook manually.

• **Anti-snipe soft-close.**  A late bidder can't insta-displace you at T-2 seconds: when a new bid arrives within 5 minutes of an expiring top-5 bid's deadline, that deadline auto-extends by 5 minutes.  The extension can fire up to 6 times per bid (30 minutes total drag), giving you real time to counter.  Your bid history shows an "Extended ×N" chip when anti-snipe has fired on one of your bids.

**Recap:** outbid = you stay queued, no refund, you get a push notification if subscribed, anti-snipe gives you time to counter, and you reappear when slots above you expire.

verify_peer_fingerprint.q: How can I be sure no one is reading my chats? (Verify peer fingerprint)
verify_peer_fingerprint.a:
Morphit chat is end-to-end encrypted by default — your messages are encrypted on your device with your counterparty's chat public key, and only their device can decrypt them.

The default trust model is "trust on first use" (TOFU): the first time you chat with someone, your client takes whatever chat key the indexer says is theirs. After that the chain-anchored pin (see "What if my chat key changed?") detects any future swap.

There's still one window where TOFU is theoretically vulnerable: the very first key exchange. A hostile indexer could, in principle, hand each side a different attacker-controlled key, so each side encrypts to the wrong person and the indexer reads everything in between. **The fingerprint feature gives you a way to detect this if you want to.**

**How to use it:**

1. Open the conversation with your counterparty.
2. Tap the ⋮ menu next to the Block button → **Verify peer**.
3. You'll see 8 words. Your counterparty does the same on their device.
4. Compare the words **out of band** — voice call, in person, or another platform you both already trust. **Do NOT compare them in this chat.**
5. If both sides see the **exact same 8 words**, no MITM occurred. You're done.
6. If even one word differs, treat the conversation as compromised. Don't continue.

**What the fingerprint protects against:**

A malicious indexer relaying fake keys to both sides simultaneously. The fingerprint is computed locally on your device from the keys actually being used to encrypt — if the indexer lied, your fingerprint and your counterparty's fingerprint won't match.

**What the fingerprint does NOT protect against:**

- **Impersonation on the OOB channel.** If you call "Bob" but the person who answers is actually Mallory, comparing fingerprints with Mallory will succeed because she controls the conversation. You have to recognize Bob's actual voice / face / handle.
- **Their device being compromised.** If Bob's phone is owned by an attacker, the attacker reads everything no matter what. Fingerprint verification can't help with that.
- **Future key changes.** Each conversation has its own fingerprint based on both sides' current keys. If your counterparty rotates their posting key (e.g. after a security incident), they get a new chat key, and the old fingerprint becomes invalid. You'd verify again with the new one.

**Privacy note:**

The fingerprint feature is opt-in. There's no badge, no banner, no nag — most users will never see this. We don't track who taps "Verify peer". The 8-word fingerprint reveals nothing about you that wasn't already public (it's derived from public keys both sides already share).

**About the OOB channel:**

Choose a channel you both already trust. Voice call works (you recognize their voice). In-person works (you can see them). Another encrypted messenger you've already verified works. SMS to a number you don't already know does NOT work — you'd be establishing trust on an unverified channel, which defeats the purpose.

If your counterparty is a stranger you've never spoken to (a new orderbook contact), fingerprint verification gives you less than it gives a contact you already know — but it still protects against indexer-side MITM, which is its job.

qr_login.q: What is QR login and is it safe?
qr_login.a: QR login lets you sign in to Morphit on a computer by scanning a code with the Morphit app on your phone — no typing your seed phrase. When you tap "Sign in with QR" on the computer, Morphit creates a one-time code that's valid for 5 minutes. You scan it with your phone, your phone shows you the website name and asks if you really did just open it on your computer, and only after you tap "Yes, that was me" does the phone send a signed permission slip back to the computer. What's safe: your private key NEVER leaves your phone. The code on the screen is a request, not a key. Even if someone screenshots the code, they can't use it without YOUR phone tapping yes. What to watch out for: when your phone asks "Sign in to morphit.io?", read the website name carefully. A scammer could send you to a fake page like "morph1t.io" (with a 1 instead of an i). Only tap Yes if YOU just opened the real Morphit on your computer. If you didn't, tap No. What this isn't: it's not a way to use Morphit without your phone. If you lose your phone you fall back to your written seed phrase. What we don't store: the operator running the website only sees an encrypted permission slip pass through. They can't read it; they can't pretend to be you.

what_is_usdt.a: USDT is a stablecoin issued by Tether Inc., designed to maintain a 1:1 peg with the US dollar. Active traders use it to park value temporarily without converting to fiat — for example, between trades, or to avoid volatility in BTC/XMR while waiting for a better entry. On Morphit you can buy and sell USDT peer-to-peer across four networks: Ethereum (ERC-20), Tron (TRC-20), Solana (SPL), and BNB Smart Chain (BEP-20). USDT is **trade-only** on Morphit — you can never pay listing fees, cold-message fees, or featured-slot bids with it. Those always cost BLURT, BTC, or XMR. The fee invariant is wire-format-frozen and enforced by sentinel smokes in CI.

why_usdt_warning.q: Why does Morphit show a chip about how USDT is issued and transmitted?
why_usdt_warning.a: USDT is the most-traded stablecoin in the world, and millions of traders rely on its dollar-stability and broad acceptance every day. When Morphit lists an asset, we tell our users about the technical properties of that asset honestly, so they can make an informed choice for each trade. For USDT, two facts worth knowing: (1) USDT is issued and administered by Tether Inc., and Tether has the technical ability to freeze addresses on the host chain — they have used this ability in the past, mostly in response to law-enforcement requests. (2) USDT transactions on every supported host chain (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BNB Smart Chain) are publicly visible on those chains; this is a property of the chain, not unique to USDT. Different traders weigh these differently. If you want maximum on-chain privacy, XMR is the right tool. If you want maximum decentralization-from-any-single-issuer with transparent chains, BTC, BLURT, BCH, or LTC are the right tools. If you want dollar-denominated stability and a market that's liquid almost anywhere, USDT is the right tool. The Morphit chip is information, not a verdict — pick the asset that fits the trade you're making.

which_usdt_network.q: Which USDT network should I pick — ERC-20, TRC-20, SPL, or BEP-20?
which_usdt_network.a: It depends on what you and your counterparty already hold and what fees you can stomach. **TRC-20 (Tron)** is the most common for P2P trades because the network fees are around $1 — predictable and cheap. **ERC-20 (Ethereum)** is the most universally accepted: every exchange, every wallet, every smart-contract platform supports it; fees are $5-20 and slower, but if your trade settles on an Ethereum-side application, this is the network to use. **SPL (Solana)** has the lowest fees (under $0.01) and is fast, but less universally accepted; pick this if you and your counterparty both use Solana wallets. **BEP-20 (BNB Smart Chain)** has fees around $0.30, fast, but less common — useful if you're moving USDT between Binance and another BSC-using counterparty. There is **no default** on Morphit — every USDT trade requires explicit network choice because cross-network sends are unrecoverable. If you send USDT-ERC20 to a TRC-20 address (or vice versa), the funds are gone forever. The network picker on the post-order form refuses to let you submit until you choose.

arbitrage_morphit_vs_exchanges.q: How does arbitrage between Morphit and centralized/decentralized exchanges work?
arbitrage_morphit_vs_exchanges.a: Morphit is built so arbitrage is easy. Listing fees are a fraction of a dollar, there's no taker fee, no withdrawal fee on the trade itself, no withdrawal limit, and no waiting period. A trader who sees a price gap between Morphit's P2P market and a CEX (Coinbase, Kraken, Binance) or DEX (Uniswap, THORChain) can post a Morphit order at a thin spread on either side and let the orderbook fill. The price-model picker lets you pin a `spread: 0.5%` against the live CoinGecko mid-price so your order tracks the market automatically — no manual re-pricing as the global price moves. As more traders use Morphit, arbitrageurs naturally pull the P2P prices into line with the broader market, which is good for everyone trading on the marketplace: tighter spreads, better fills, more predictable execution. A few practical notes: Morphit's per-trade settlement is what you make it — direct wallet-to-wallet for crypto-vs-crypto pairs (XMR for USDT, BTC for USDT), or via your bank/fiat rail of choice for crypto-vs-fiat. For high-frequency arbitrage, the Sybil-tier fee structure escalates listing costs if you post many orders quickly from the same account; this is anti-spam infrastructure, not anti-arbitrage — most arbitrageurs run a single account per direction and never hit the tier-2 threshold.

privacy_terms.heading: Privacy & Terms
privacy_terms.privacy_body_1: Morphit runs in your browser. Your keys are generated on your device and never leave it. Morphit does not collect tracking cookies, analytics, or your IP address for any purpose beyond what's technically required to serve the page.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_2: Everything you post to the orderbook — offers, feedback, chats — is public on a permanent decentralized network. Once it's posted, it's there forever.
privacy_terms.privacy_body_3: We encourage you to use a VPN, Tor, Lokinet, or I2P when accessing Morphit — anything that hides your IP from the server you're talking to is a good idea. We don't fingerprint your browser, we don't profile you, and we explicitly design our defenses against abuse so they don't punish privacy-conscious users. Our rate limits are crude (a handful of signups per IP per day) and easily defeated by VPN rotation — that's a conscious tradeoff. We'd rather accept more abuse than make privacy-respecting users feel unwelcome. If a defense would require tracking you to work, we don't ship it.

run_a_node.title: Run a Morphit node
run_a_node.subtitle: Operate your own instance. Earn a share of listing fees. Help make Morphit uncensorable.
run_a_node.why_uncensor_body: Every additional node makes the network harder to censor. If your country blocks morphit.io, your instance stays reachable. You serve users who'd otherwise have no way to trade.
run_a_node.why_community_body: Brand the interface for your region, your language, your local payment methods. Users trust frontends that speak their language and feel familiar — yours will.
run_a_node.why_privacy_body: Users trading through your instance share metadata with you and only you. No other operator, not even Agorise, sees their activity patterns.
run_a_node.why_earn_body:
Every BLURT-paid listing fee your instance attracts pays you 90% — only 10% goes to the Morphit treasury to fund welcome bonuses, loyalty delegations, and account-creation costs. BTC- and XMR-paid fees flow 100% to the treasury for the same project obligations (the on-chain split mechanism only works for BLURT, but we made the BLURT split aggressively generous to compensate — 90/10 in your favor instead of the 50/50 we considered originally).

A Smart Contract running on the Blurt chain enforces the split — not a person, not a company, not anyone who can change their mind. 100% automated. No invoices, no payouts, no trust assumptions. You provably assist, you provably get paid. Guaranteed in code.

Payouts are denominated in BLURT, so if BLURT appreciates, so do your earnings — without any additional work on your part. Fully open source under AGPL-3.0; if you can read the indexer source, you can audit the payout logic.
run_a_node.step1_body: Linux (Debian 12, Ubuntu 22.04+, Arch, NixOS — we test on Debian). 2 CPU cores at 1 GHz+, 2 GB RAM minimum (4 GB comfortable), 20 GB SSD. A Raspberry Pi 4, an old laptop, or a $5/month VPS all work. No static IP needed — DDNS works fine. See the FAQ entry on minimum hardware requirements for the full breakdown across hobbyist, serious, and spare-laptop tiers.
run_a_node.step2_body: Fork or clone git.agorise.net/agorise/morphit. Copy env examples from ops/env/, set your domain, set the indexer's RPC endpoints (Blurt public nodes work out of the box).
run_a_node.step3_body: systemd units for the indexer and relay are in ops/systemd/. nginx config with TLS is in ops/nginx/. Run the migration tool once to initialize the database schema.
run_a_node.step4_body: Run the register-operator CLI tool with your chosen tag (1-64 chars, alphanumeric + dashes/underscores/dots). Tags are first-come-first-served — once you broadcast the one-time `morphit_register_operator` op, that tag is yours. Your instance appears in /operators and begins attributing orders (and earning your 90% share of BLURT-paid listing fees) immediately. See the operator-earnings FAQ for the full economics.
run_a_node.asset_policy_body: Morphit's federation lets each operator pick which tradable assets their instance accepts new orders for. New assets ship default-ON instance-wide — operators opt out per-asset via the `MORPHIT_INDEXER_DISABLED_ASSETS` environment variable. This is how a federation of instances can serve different user preferences without anyone needing to fork the code.
run_a_node.asset_policy_default_body: When the project adds a new tradable asset (USDT shipped most recently), every instance accepts orders for it the moment they upgrade. No code change, no per-asset enablement step.
run_a_node.asset_policy_opt_out_body: Operators who prefer their instance specializes in privacy-first or decentralization-first assets can disable any trade-only asset with `MORPHIT_INDEXER_DISABLED_ASSETS="USDT"` (or a comma-separated list for multiple). Users posting through this operator's frontend then can't pick a disabled asset.
run_a_node.asset_policy_federation_body: Disabling an asset on your instance doesn't hide peer instances' orders from your users — chain history is shared, so the orderbook still surfaces them as read-only. The gate is only on NEW orders posted FROM your instance.

download.web_body: Morphit works fully in any mobile browser. Firefox, Brave, Tor Browser for Android — pick one and go. No install, no permissions, no app-store relationship of any kind.
download.iphone_body: Yes, iPhone users can use Morphit fully — no jailbreak needed. Apple's App Store doesn't list non-KYC peer-to-peer crypto apps, so there's no native iOS app. Instead, you install Morphit as a Progressive Web App (PWA) through Safari. The result behaves like a regular app: home-screen icon, fullscreen launch, offline-capable browsing.
download.iphone_step_1: Open this site in Safari (not Chrome or Firefox — only Safari can install PWAs on iOS).
download.iphone_step_2: Tap the Share icon (the square with an up-arrow at the bottom of the screen).
download.iphone_step_3: Scroll down and tap "Add to Home Screen."
download.iphone_step_4: Tap "Add" in the top-right. Morphit's icon now lives on your Home Screen and launches in fullscreen mode.
download.iphone_jailbreak_note: iOS 16.4 or newer recommended for full PWA support (service workers, push notifications). Older iOS versions still work — the icon installs and the site loads — but with reduced offline capability.
download.operator_section_subtitle: Anyone can run a Morphit node — your own brand, your own users, your own fee revenue. The federation finds you automatically. Below is everything you need.
download.operator_source_body: Morphit is AGPL-3.0. Clone the repo, run the smoke suite, deploy. Each release is signed and its SHA-256 manifest is published on the Blurt chain so you can verify what you cloned matches what the project published.
download.operator_verify_note: Every release artifact (APK, source tarball, container image) has its SHA-256 hash recorded on the Blurt chain via a `morphit_release_v1` op. Verify any download by re-hashing locally and comparing against the on-chain manifest. The chain doesn't lie.
download.operator_setup_body: We don't ship pre-built `.deb` or `.rpm` packages — Morphit is a multi-component server (Postgres + Node.js indexer + relay + reverse proxy) and one-package installs would hide the architecture from you. Instead, the operator handbook walks you through it step-by-step.
download.operator_setup_doc_ops: OPERATIONS.md — ongoing operator runbook (backups, top-ups, RPC management)
download.operator_setup_doc_switching: SWITCHING-NETWORKS.md — staging procedure + going-live launch checklist
download.operator_distros_body: Tested on Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04+, but should work on any modern Linux (Arch, Alpine, NixOS) with Node.js 22+ and Postgres 15+. FreeBSD works with minor adjustments. Hardware: any 2-core ARM64 or x86-64 machine with 4 GB RAM and 20 GB SSD — most operators run on a Raspberry Pi 4, an Intel mini-PC, or a spare laptop.
download.operator_join_body: Once your instance is live and broadcasting `morphit_operator_register_v1`, it appears in every other Morphit instance's directory automatically. No application, no permission, no central listing.

backup_keys.title: Back up your keys
backup_keys.subtitle: This is the most important page on Morphit. Read it before you need it.
backup_keys.reality_lead: Morphit is non-custodial. Nobody — not us, not your operator, not any support agent anywhere — can help you recover your account if you lose your keys.
backup_keys.reality_body:
There is no 'forgot password' link. There is no 'verify with ID' process. There is no backup account on a server somewhere. Your keys exist in two places: this device (right now) and wherever you copy them to. That's the entire list.

Lose the keys, lose the account. Lose the funds. Lose the reputation you built from every trade. No exceptions, no appeals, no human on Earth can intervene.

This is the tradeoff for a service that does not, and cannot, seize your money or freeze your account. The same thing that keeps you safe from us keeps you exposed to your own mistakes.
backup_keys.reality_slogan: In the crypto world, YOU are the bank.
backup_keys.what_heading: What to back up, and how
backup_keys.seed_body:
Your seed phrase is a standard BIP-39 mnemonic — 12 words, generated during onboarding. Any BIP-39-compatible wallet in the world can regenerate your keys from it. This is your ultimate recovery.

If you didn't write it down during onboarding, it's gone. We cannot regenerate it. Your keys were derived from it before it was wiped from memory.
backup_keys.seed_tip_paper: Write it on paper. Two copies, stored in two separate physical locations.
backup_keys.seed_tip_steel: For amounts you care about, stamp it into a steel backup plate. Paper burns and gets waterlogged.
backup_keys.seed_tip_split: For larger balances, split it: first 6 words in one location, last 6 in another. Both halves together = full access. Neither half alone = nothing.
backup_keys.seed_tip_digital_warning: Never store the seed in email, cloud notes, screenshots, password managers synced to a cloud, or any app that can be remotely accessed.
backup_keys.keyfile_body: Your session was booted with a password-encrypted keyfile. Re-download it now and store it somewhere separate from the device you're using. If you forget the password, the keyfile is useless — so treat the password as equally critical.
backup_keys.keyfile_locked_hint: Sign in first to download your encrypted keyfile. This page still works without signing in for the education.
backup_keys.keyfile_download_err_locked: Your session appears to be locked. Sign in to download your keyfile.
backup_keys.redundancy_body:
The crypto survivors are the ones who planned for fire, flood, death, and their own forgetfulness.

Two physical copies of your seed phrase in separate locations. At least one in a safe or safety deposit box. Consider an estate plan: how does a trusted heir find your keys if something happens to you? Write down the instructions separately from the keys themselves.

Redundancy costs you 10 minutes of effort. Its absence can cost you everything.
backup_keys.antipatterns_heading: Common mistakes that cost people everything
backup_keys.anti_email: Emailing the seed phrase to yourself. Any breach of your email provider exposes it.
backup_keys.anti_cloud: Storing the seed in Google Drive, iCloud, Dropbox, OneDrive. These are searched by automated malware, subpoenaed by governments, breached by attackers.
backup_keys.anti_photo: Taking a photo of the seed. Your photos sync to the cloud. Your phone gets stolen. The photo leaks.
backup_keys.anti_share: Sharing the seed with 'support' — ours, or anyone else's. Real support never, ever asks for your seed. Anyone who does is a scammer.
backup_keys.anti_support: Assuming someone can help you recover. They can't. We can't. Nobody can. This is the whole point of non-custodial.

security.keys_title: Your keys never leave your device.
security.keys_body: Keys are generated in your browser using libsodium. They are encrypted with a password you choose (Argon2id + XSalsa20-Poly1305) before being stored. No Morphit server ever sees them.
security.tracking_body: No cookies. No analytics. No third-party scripts. No IP logging. No telemetry. If you look at the Network tab in your browser, every request goes to Morphit and nowhere else.
security.chat_body: Every message uses X25519 key agreement plus ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption (libsodium primitives) with a fresh ephemeral key per message. Plaintext exists only inside your browser and your trading partner's browser. Morphit's servers, the Blurt blockchain, and anyone in between see only ciphertext. The full protocol — including the deliberate tradeoffs we accept (no per-message forward secrecy) — is in {chat_crypto_doc}.
security.reproducible_body: Every release is tagged; every asset is fingerprinted; SRI protects every script. You can rebuild from source and compare — we publish the hashes alongside each release.
security.open_source_body: The full threat model is in the repo's {security_doc}. We're explicit about what we protect against and what we don't — because pretending otherwise would be worse than honesty.
security.footer_body: Found an issue? Please report via the public Forgejo repo, or (in Phase 5) via an encrypted message to the {morphit_account} account on Blurt.
security.bounty_body: We run a discretionary security recognition program. Every actionable finding gets reviewed by a real engineer, gets an answer, and — if it materially improves Morphit's security posture — gets rewarded in BLURT (paid from @morphit-fees) or BTC, scaled to severity and the report's quality. No fixed tier table; case-by-case adjudication. Hall of fame credit available even when payment isn't. The full scope, severity guidance, payment workflow, and what we won't do (no NDA, no exclusive disclosure) is documented in SECURITY.md.
security.bounty_link: Read the full bounty program scope and rules →
security.canary_body: We publish a weekly warrant canary signed with the operator's PGP key. The canary explicitly declares no NSL / FISA / gag-order / backdoor demand has been served. Freshness proofs include a current Blurt chain head, a current Bitcoin chain head, and a current news headline (proves the canary cannot be pre-generated). If the canary stops updating for more than 14 days, treat it as silent: the operator may be under coercive pressure, and you should switch to a different federated operator.

active_key.title: Active key
active_key.body: One of the three private keys your Morphit account has. The active key is for moving BLURT — paying listing fees, sending tips, transferring balances. Morphit asks for it (or rather, for the password that unlocks it on your device) only when you're about to spend. It never leaves your browser.

blurt.title: BLURT
blurt.body: BLURT is two things: a blockchain (where Morphit's order ops, fees, and chat ciphertext live), and the asset you pay listing fees with. The asset and the chain share the same name. There is no Morphit token — Morphit uses BLURT directly.

blurt_power.title: BLURT Power
blurt_power.body: BLURT that you have "powered up" — staked into your account so it can't be spent immediately. BLURT Power gives you weight when voting on Blurt content (separate from Morphit) and is the basis for delegation. Morphit doesn't require any BLURT Power to use; it matters mainly if you syndicate trade announcements to the wider Blurt community.

broadcast.title: Broadcast
broadcast.body: To send a signed operation to the Blurt blockchain. Posting an order, cancelling an order, leaving feedback, sending an encrypted chat message — all of these are broadcasts. Once a broadcast lands in a block, it can't be undone (the operation is on-chain forever); only superseded by a later one.

counterparty.title: Counterparty
counterparty.body: The other person in a trade. If you posted a sell order and someone messages you to buy, that person is your counterparty. The word is neutral — it doesn't mean "opponent." Both sides of every Morphit trade have a counterparty: each is the other's.

custom_json.title: custom_json
custom_json.body: A type of operation on the Blurt blockchain that carries arbitrary structured data. Morphit's order ops, feedback ops, chat envelopes, and operator registrations are all custom_json operations — they ride on the chain's existing infrastructure rather than requiring a new chain. You don't need to interact with custom_json directly; Morphit builds them for you.

delegation.title: Delegation
delegation.body: Lending some of your BLURT Power to another account temporarily, without giving them control of the underlying BLURT. Morphit doesn't require delegation to use, but operators sometimes delegate to new accounts to give them initial weight. Delegations can be undone (with a cooldown period before the BLURT Power becomes liquid again).

federation.title: Federation
federation.body: Multiple independent Morphit instances that share the same orderbook and chat ecosystem because they all read from the same Blurt blockchain. If one operator goes offline (or hostile), users move to another and find the same orders, the same trades, the same reputations. Federation is what makes Morphit uncensorable.

feedback.title: Feedback
feedback.body: A signed, on-chain rating you leave for a counterparty after a trade. Feedback is permanent — it can't be deleted, only responded to. Your reputation in Morphit is the sum of feedback others have left for you over time. Both sides of every completed trade are entitled to leave one piece of feedback.

fiat.title: Fiat
fiat.body: Government-issued currency: dollars, euros, yen, pesos, rubles. The opposite of crypto. On Morphit, fiat is what changes hands off-platform — you and your counterparty agree on a price in fiat (e.g. USD), settle the fiat side privately (cash, bank transfer, your choice), and Morphit handles only the crypto side.

indexer.title: Indexer
indexer.body: The component of a Morphit instance that watches the Blurt blockchain, decodes Morphit-relevant operations (orders, feedback, chat envelopes), and serves them to the web frontend in a usable shape. The chain is the source of truth; the indexer is just a fast cache. Run by the operator, not by you.

listing_fee.title: Listing fee
listing_fee.body: The small BLURT fee Morphit charges when you post a new order. The fee covers operator costs and disincentivizes spam orderbooks. The first order from a new account is free. Listing fees scale gently with how often you post. Cancelling an order does NOT refund the listing fee — it's the cost of the listing, not the trade.

network_fee.title: Network fee
network_fee.body: Two unrelated things share this name in casual speech: (1) Morphit's listing fee — the BLURT cost of posting an order; and (2) the Bitcoin or Monero on-chain fee that miners take when you settle the crypto side of a trade. Morphit only ever charges the first; the second is between you and the underlying network when you make the actual transfer.

operator.title: Operator
operator.body: The person or team running a particular Morphit instance — the website you're looking at right now is operated by someone. The operator runs the indexer and relay servers, sets policies for their instance (rate limits, fee tiers, kill-switch), and earns a share of the listing fees that flow through. If an operator goes hostile, you can switch to a different instance and find your same orders, same trades, same reputation.

password.title: Password
password.body: What unlocks your private keys on your device. Morphit never sees, sends, stores, or knows your password — it's used locally by your browser to decrypt the encrypted bundle of keys held in your browser's storage. If you forget your password, the keys are gone; that's why Morphit asks you to write down your seed phrase during onboarding.

permlink.title: Permlink
permlink.body: The unique short identifier of an order on the Blurt blockchain — something like `morphit-o-2k4f9`. Permlinks let you (and the chain, and other Morphit instances) refer to a specific order without ambiguity. The order's URL on any Morphit instance ends in its permlink, so order links are portable across instances.

posting_key.title: Posting key
posting_key.body: Another of your account's three private keys. The posting key is for signing content — chat messages, feedback, comments. It's lower-trust than the active key (it can't move BLURT) so a compromise is less catastrophic. Morphit uses it for chat-payload signing and feedback ops; you'll never need to handle it directly.

relay.title: Relay
relay.body: The component of a Morphit instance that handles things the indexer can't — chat envelope acceptance, fee verification, kill-switch enforcement, anti-spam policies. The relay is the moving-parts side of an instance (the indexer is read-only against the chain). Run by the operator, not by you.

release_op.title: Release op
release_op.body: An on-chain operation broadcast by the @morphit account that publishes the bundle hashes for a new Morphit release. Frontend pages use it to verify they're running unmodified code: each page hashes its own bundle and checks that the hash is signed off in a recent release_op. If the hashes don't match, the page warns you that the operator may be serving tampered code.

seed_phrase.title: Seed phrase
seed_phrase.body: Twelve English words that, taken together, are the master backup of your account. From the seed phrase your device can re-derive every key your account has. If your device dies and you lose your password, the seed phrase is what gets you back in. Write it down on paper. Don't take a screenshot. Don't email it to yourself. Don't store it in a password manager that lives on the same device.

sign.title: Sign
sign.body: To attach a cryptographic signature to a piece of data using one of your private keys, proving the data came from you and hasn't been altered. When Morphit asks you to "unlock to sign," it's about to ask the chain to accept an action on your behalf — posting an order, sending a message, paying a fee. The signing happens locally on your device; the private key never leaves.

first_post_starter.heading: Your first order? Some safer defaults
first_post_starter.intro: We've pre-filled a few choices to make your first listing safer. You can change any of them below.
first_post_starter.tip_small_body: A small first trade (under $50) limits what you can lose if something goes wrong. You can post bigger orders once you've built reputation through completed trades.
first_post_starter.tip_expiry_body: We've set the expiry to 7 days instead of the default 90. A shorter window means stale offers don't linger if you change your mind.
first_post_starter.tip_payment_body: Add the payment methods you actually accept. Trade partners pick which works for them. Common starting points: PayPal, Wise, bank transfer, cash in person.

cheat_sheet.heading: Morphit cheat-sheet
cheat_sheet.intro: A one-page reference for the things grandmas keep mixing up. Print it and keep it next to the keyboard.
cheat_sheet.subtitle: Quick reference for everything you'll be asked while using Morphit.
cheat_sheet.footer: Morphit · morphit.io · open source · AGPL-3.0 · keep this paper safe.

section_identity.heading: Account name vs seed phrase vs password
section_identity.account_name_body: Your public name on the Blurt chain (e.g. @alice). Other people see this. Choosing a new one is permanent — costs ~3 BLURT.
section_identity.seed_phrase_body: 12 words. The ONLY way back into your account if you lose your device. Anyone who has them owns your account. Write them on paper, store somewhere safe.
section_identity.password_body: Just for THIS device, not the chain. Encrypts your seed in this browser. If you forget it, type your seed phrase to log in again. Different from the seed.

section_fees.heading: Listing fee vs network fee vs trade payment
section_fees.listing_fee_body: What Morphit charges to publish your order. Tiny — about 60 BLURT (~$0.12). First buy: free. Pay in BLURT, BTC, or XMR.
section_fees.network_fee_body: What the Bitcoin or Monero network charges to confirm a payment. Goes to miners, not Morphit. Varies — check the wallet you send from.
section_fees.trade_payment_body: The actual money you send (or receive) for the trade. Morphit never holds it — straight from buyer to seller, off-platform.

section_assets.heading: Supported tradable assets
section_assets.btc: Bitcoin. Most known. Public ledger — anyone can see who paid whom. Fees vary widely.
section_assets.xmr: Monero. Private — no one can see who paid whom. Fees usually low. The privacy choice.
section_assets.blurt: The token of the Blurt blockchain that Morphit runs on. Used to pay listing fees, post messages, sign orders.
section_assets.usdt: Tether stablecoin. Pegged 1:1 to USD. Trade across four networks: ERC-20 (Ethereum), TRC-20 (Tron), SPL (Solana), BEP-20 (BNB Smart Chain). Pick the network before sending — cross-network is unrecoverable.
section_assets.bch: BCH — Bitcoin Cash, transparent, decentralized, bigger blocks than BTC
section_assets.ltc: LTC — Litecoin, fast, low-fee Bitcoin fork (since 2011). Trade-only on Morphit. Use a Litecoin wallet (Electrum-LTC, Litewallet, hardware wallets); accepts L… legacy, M… modern P2SH, and ltc1… SegWit addresses.

section_recovery.heading: If something goes wrong
section_recovery.lost_seed_body: There is no recovery path. Morphit has no copy. If you still have access to the device, move funds out NOW and start a new account.
section_recovery.lost_password_body: Click "Sign in" and choose "Import seed phrase". Type your 12 words. Set a new password.
section_recovery.lost_device_body: On a new device, go to morphit.io, click "Sign in", choose "Import seed phrase", type your 12 words. Set a new password.
section_recovery.suspect_compromise_body: Move funds to a new account immediately. Anyone with the seed has full control. There's no "freeze" button on a blockchain.

Transactions are publicly visible on each supported network (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BNB Smart Chain) — a property of those chains. Pick the asset that fits your trade.

privacy.index_meta_description: How to make your trades more private on transparent and private chains. Per-asset guidance covering fresh addresses, opt-in privacy tech, and common pitfalls.
privacy.index_intro: Most assets traded on Morphit (BTC, BCH, LTC, BLURT, USDT) live on transparent chains — any observer can read the chain history. There are concrete steps you can take to make YOUR trades much harder to link, profile, or surveil. This is registry-driven: the next asset Morphit adds will get a guide automatically.
privacy.section_fresh_addresses: Use a fresh address every trade
privacy.section_opt_in_tech_intro: Standards that wallets in this ecosystem may implement. Morphit does NOT recommend specific wallet software — even reputable wallets have been compromised. Search for a wallet that supports these standards and review its trust posture yourself.
privacy.no_wallet_recommendation: Morphit does NOT recommend specific wallet software. Even reputable wallets have been compromised or have had hidden flaws. The privacy techniques here are protocol standards, not endorsements — your wallet, your responsibility.

fresh_address_advice.subaddress: This chain supports stealth/subaddress technology natively. Your wallet derives a fresh receive address (subaddress) per trade from your view key. The recipient sees a unique address every time; chain observers cannot link multiple trades to the same wallet.
fresh_address_advice.hd-derived: This chain uses transparent addresses with no native stealth. The standard practice: use a Hierarchical Deterministic (BIP-32) wallet that derives a new receive address per request. Most modern wallets do this automatically. The cost of address reuse is severe — every trade you accept at the same address builds a public record of your activity.
fresh_address_advice.account-reuse: This chain is account-based — your account name is your address. Fresh-account-per-trade is not practical (each new account costs chain resources). Accept that this asset has the highest amount-correlation risk on Morphit. For high-value trades, consider using an alt-account dedicated to that trade.

mweb.name: MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks)
mweb.explain: A native Litecoin protocol-level privacy feature. MWEB hides transaction amounts and breaks the address-to-amount link for transfers that opt in. Per-transaction; not chain-wide. Look for wallets that surface "MWEB" or "Extension Blocks" as an option when sending.

cashfusion.name: CashFusion
cashfusion.explain: A Bitcoin Cash CoinJoin variant designed by the BCH community. Mixes inputs and outputs of varying amounts to defeat both common-input-ownership and amount-correlation heuristics. Run from a wallet that supports CashFusion before or after a trade to launder the on-chain history.

coinjoin.name: CoinJoin
coinjoin.explain: A family of protocols where multiple participants pool inputs and outputs into a single transaction, breaking the common-input-ownership heuristic that links coins to one owner. Multiple implementations exist with different trust models — choose carefully and read the implementation's threat model.

payjoin.name: PayJoin (BIP-78)
payjoin.explain: A two-party cooperative transaction protocol. Sender and receiver both contribute inputs, so chain observers cannot apply the standard "all inputs come from the same wallet" heuristic. Morphit's address-share modal includes an optional PayJoin endpoint field — if both wallets support BIP-78, the trade automatically uses PayJoin.

common_practices.fresh_per_trade: **Use a fresh receive address for every trade.** Your wallet should support this; if it doesn't, look for one that does. Address reuse is the single biggest leak.
common_practices.coin_control: **Practice coin control when spending.** When sending coins later, avoid combining the trade output with coins from another source — that combines their address histories permanently.
common_practices.network_layer: **Broadcast through Tor or your wallet's privacy mode.** Your home IP address sees the transaction first; nodes near your IP can correlate it to you. A Tor-aware wallet broadcasts through Tor by default.
common_practices.kyc_touchpoints: **Avoid sending trade coins to or from KYC exchanges.** Once trade coins touch a KYC exchange, the trade becomes legally identifiable by combining exchange records with chain data. If you need to bridge to fiat, route through a self-custodied intermediate step.

what_not_to_do.reuse_address: Do not paste your same receive address into multiple trades.
what_not_to_do.exact_amount: Do not send the exact amount listed on the order — Morphit's amount-randomizer toggle (the "🔐 Randomize amount" checkbox in the address-share modal) breaks this; leave it ON.
what_not_to_do.combine_utxos: Do not combine the trade output with coins from a different source when you later spend it.
what_not_to_do.clearnet_broadcast: Do not broadcast from your home IP via a non-private wallet — use Tor.

btc.one_line: Transparent chain, fully decentralized — opt-in mixing protocols available.
btc.intro: Bitcoin is the most-analyzed chain in the world. Every transaction is public; every address can be tracked over time. The privacy practices below dramatically reduce how easily a third party can profile your trades — without requiring you to leave BTC.
btc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, PayJoin, CoinJoin, and what to avoid.

xmr.one_line: Privacy by default — stealth addresses, hidden amounts, ring signatures.
xmr.intro: Monero is the strongest privacy posture on Morphit. By default, your address, amount, and counterparty are hidden from third parties. The practices below are minor tightenings; the chain itself does the heavy lifting.
xmr.meta_description: Privacy practices for Monero trades on Morphit: subaddresses and amount handling.

blurt.one_line: Coordination chain — transparent and account-based. Lowest privacy on Morphit.
blurt.intro: BLURT is Morphit's coordination chain — orders, chat ciphertexts, fees, and reputation all live here. The chain is fully public and account-based, meaning every BLURT transfer involving your account is permanently visible to anyone. There is no opt-in privacy technology for BLURT.
blurt.caveats: BLURT is structurally the least private asset on Morphit. Your account name is your address; you cannot rotate it. For trades where on-chain privacy matters more than speed and cost, prefer XMR, BTC (with PayJoin), BCH (with CashFusion), or LTC (with MWEB).
blurt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for BLURT trades on Morphit: account-based chain, transparent by design.

usdt.one_line: Centralized — Tether can freeze any address. Transparent on every chain.
usdt.intro: USDT's privacy issue is structurally different from the other transparent assets: it's centralized. Tether Inc. can freeze any USDT address on any host chain, and they have used this ability in the past. No amount of address rotation or transaction obfuscation changes Tether's freeze capability.
usdt.caveats: Even with perfect on-chain privacy practices, USDT remains centrally freezable. Practical on-chain privacy on USDT host chains (Ethereum, Tron, Solana, BSC) is the same as on any transparent EVM/UTXO/account chain — your privacy depends on the host chain's opt-in privacy ecosystem (Tornado Cash on ETH, etc.), which we do not endorse or describe further here.
usdt.meta_description: Privacy considerations for USDT trades on Morphit: centralization risk and host-chain transparency.

bch.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — CashFusion provides opt-in mixing.
bch.intro: Bitcoin Cash shares Bitcoin's transparency model: every transaction visible on chain, every address linkable. CashFusion (a BCH-community CoinJoin variant with amount-randomization) is the main opt-in privacy technology and is well-integrated into several BCH wallets.
bch.meta_description: Privacy practices for Bitcoin Cash trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, CashFusion, and what to avoid.

ltc.one_line: Transparent, decentralized — MWEB provides opt-in chain-level privacy.
ltc.intro: Litecoin shares Bitcoin's transparency at the base layer, but adds MWEB (MimbleWimble Extension Blocks) — a chain-level opt-in privacy feature that hides amounts and breaks address linkability for transfers that opt in. This is the closest a Bitcoin-family chain comes to native privacy.
ltc.meta_description: Privacy practices for Litecoin trades on Morphit: fresh addresses, MWEB, and what to avoid.
